lay_term: The provider performs a secondary repair of a cleft lip and or nasal deformity. The provider performs this service if a primary repair of a cleft lip and or nasal deformity does not deliver favorable results. In this procedure, the provider reopens the defect and recloses the surgical site. Unfavorable results can include scar contracture, a tightening of the skin and or shortening of the muscle that restricts movement, the wound splitting or layers separating, and infection. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the margins of the cleft surface from the mouth to the nostril to create clean edges for the defect. The provider performs this procedure to surgically repair the results of the primary cleft lip and or nasal deformity closure. He carries the incision through the full thickness of the mucosa, muscle, and skin. He brings the muscles and skin together to close the separation while maintaining muscle function and symmetry. He closes the prepared margins on either side in layers from the intraoral mucosa through the muscle, and finally he closes the skin. Terminology Cleft lip: A condition present from birth, in which there is a split in the upper lip on one or both sides. Mucosa: A membrane that lines many body cavities and organs; also called mucus membrane; it secretes mucus. Tips When coding a primary cleft lip repair, also known as cheiloplasty, there are several codes to choose. Review all codes before determining the code to report. See 40700, Plastic repair of cleft lip or nasal deformity; primary, partial or complete, unilateral, 40701, Plastic repair of cleft lip or nasal deformity; primary bilateral, 1 stage procedure, or 40702, Plastic repair of cleft lip and or nasal deformity; primary bilateral, one stage procedure, depending on whether the surgery is unilateral or bilateral and the provider performs the service in one or two stages. In addition, look to 40720 and 40761, Plastic repair of cleft lip and or nasal deformity; with cross lip pedicle flap (Abbe Estlander type), including sectioning and inserting of pedicle, to determine the code to report. short_description: Excision of lesion of mucosa and submucosa, vestibule of mouth; with simple repair
lay_term: The provider excises a lesion or area of damaged or diseased tissue of the mucosa, a membrane lining the anterior most part of the mouth, and the submucosa, the layer beneath the mucosa. This procedure involves a simple repair of the surgical wound. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the lesion with a scalpel or needle tipped electrocautery in the mucosa and or submucosa of the affected vestibule area of the patient’s mouth. He then removes the lesion along with its margins. The provider closes the small, superficial defects with one layer of simple, interrupted sutures. Terminology Cyst: A closed, sac like area within tissue that has a distinct membrane and may contain liquid, gaseous, or semisolid substances; cysts vary in size and there are many types, including benign and malignant, and can be found in many locations in the body; also a bladder such as a the urinary bladder or gallbladder. Electrocautery: Stoppage of bleeding using a needle or other instrument that is electrically heated. Epinephrine: A hormone secreted in the human body; it causes the heart to beat faster, strengthens the force of the heart's contraction, and opens up the airways in the lungs. Gingivobuccal groove: The upper and lower half of the oral vestibule on each side of the mouth. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Mucosa: A membrane that lines many body cavities and organs; it’s also called mucus membrane; it secretes mucus. Neuroma: A mass formed on a nerve, usually symptomless but sometimes harmful. Nodule: A small swelling or aggregation of cells in the body, commonly abnormal. Periosteum: A dense layer of flexible tissue enveloping the bones except at the surfaces of the joints. Scalpel: Surgical knife. Submucosa: The layer of tissue lying beneath a mucosa. Vestibule of mouth: A thin space between the teeth and gums, and the lips and cheeks; it does not include the teeth. Tips An example of the use of 40812 occurs when the provider injects a patient with lidocaine, an anesthetic or pain killer and epinephrine. The provider uses an antiseptic on the skin, and then in the gingivobuccal groove. He uses electrocautery to make an incision in the mucosa, and elevates the soft tissue off the periosteum. The provider identifies the nerve, finds a small nodule most consistent with a neuroma, transects it, and closes the wound. The correct code to report this service is 40812. A diagnosis would be helpful in determining the correct code, but the term gingivobuccal groove, also known as the alveolobuccal groove, gives away the general location in the vestibule of the mouth: between the lips and the teeth. The provider merely sews up the wound, so report a simple repair rather than 40814, Excision of lesion of mucosa and submucosa, vestibule of mouth; with complex repair or 40816, Excision of lesion of mucosa and submucosa, vestibule of mouth; complex, with excision of underlying muscle. short_description: Vestibuloplasty; anterior
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider improves the height of the alveolar ridge by various methods. This code applies to anterior, or front, vestibuloplasty. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins the procedure to make the vestibule of the mouth deeper, which in turn improves the height of the alveolar ridge. In an example procedure, the provider dissects the mucosa from the anterior aspect of the vestibule of the mouth and frees the tissue from the bone. She moves the mucosa deep into the mouth and rearranges tissue as needed. She may also place a splint in the mouth, which she will remove at a later office visit. This procedure may help patients whose anatomy makes it difficult to wear dental devices such as dentures or in patient’s requiring reconstructive surgery after trauma or removal of lesions. Terminology Alveolar ridge: A ridge like border on the upper and lower jaw from where the teeth arise. Anterior: Closer to the front part of the body. Vestibule of mouth: Also called oral vestibule; the space in the mouth between the cheeks and the teeth. Vestibuloplasty: A surgical modification of the oral cavity to restore the height of the alveolar ridge. Tips Use 40842 if the provider performs posterior vestibuloplasty on one side of the mouth. Use 40843 if the provider performs posterior vestibuloplasty on both sides of the mouth. Use 40844 if the provider performs vestibuloplasty of the entire arch. Use 40845 if the provider performs a complex vestibuloplasty, including ridge extension or muscle repositioning. Read Less

short_description: Vestibuloplasty; complex (including ridge extension, muscle repositioning) Notes: (For skin grafts, see 15002 et seq)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider improves the height of the alveolar ridge by various methods. This code applies to complex vestibuloplasty, which may involve extending the ridge or lowering specific muscles. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins the procedure to make the vestibule of the mouth deeper, which in turn improves the height of the alveolar ridge. In an example procedure, the provider makes an incision in the mucosal layer over the alveolar ridge. The provider excises the extra mucosa or may reposition it. She brings the incision down to the muscles and detaches the muscles. The provider then lengthens and reattaches the muscles, thereby further widening the vestibule of the mouth. The provider checks for any bleeding, removes all the instruments, and closes the incision in the alveolar ridge sites with sutures in layers. This procedure may help patients whose anatomy makes it difficult to wear dental devices such as dentures or in patients requiring reconstructive surgery after trauma or removal of lesions. Terminology Alveolar ridge: A ridge like border on the upper and lower jaw containing tooth sockets. Oral mucosa: Membrane lining the mouth. Vestibule of mouth: Also called oral vestibule; the space in the mouth between the cheeks and the teeth. Vestibuloplasty: A surgical modification of the oral cavity to restore the height of the alveolar ridge. Tips For anterior vestibuloplasty, use 40840, Vestibuloplasty; anterior. For vestibuloplasty on one side of the back jaw, use 40842, Vestibuloplasty; posterior, bilateral. For vestibuloplasty on both sides of the back jaw, use 40843, Vestibuloplasty; posterior, bilateral. short_description: Glossectomy; composite procedure with resection floor of mouth, mandibular resection, and radical neck dissection (Commando type)
lay_term: The provider removes all or part of the tongue, as well as part of the jaw bone (mandible) and the tissue of the floor of the mouth using extraoral (outside the mouth) and intraoral (inside the mouth) incisions. This code also includes removal of lymph nodes and other tissues from one side of the neck. This procedure is most often used to treat cancer. Explanation The provider performs glossectomy where he removes all or part of the tongue, cauterizing tissue as needed to help control bleeding. He removes the tongue and sutures the wound closed. To access the diseased tissue, the provider makes incisions inside and outside the mouth. He also removes affected tissue from the mandible (jaw bone) and floor of the mouth. After removing the affected portions of the mandible, the surgeon places a metal plate or bone graft to reestablish continuity of the mandible. If needed, the metal plate is replaced with a bone graft during a later procedure. This code also includes removal of lymph nodes and other tissues from one side of the neck. The physician closes the incisions with sutures, which might include skin or mucosal grafts. This procedure is most often used to treat cancer. Terminology Glossectomy: Surgical removal of all or a part of the tongue, also known as lingulectomy. Hyoid bone: A small bone at the base of the lower jaw that is shaped like the letter U and serves to support the tongue to facilitate speech and swallowing; it is the only bone in the human body that does not connect to any other bone and is instead connected only through muscle tissue. Lymph nodes: Small nodules at various points along the circulation of the lymph system; the lymph system returns fluid from the spaces between tissues back to the blood stream and supports the immune system. Radical resection (or dissection): Surgical removal of a structure to include its vascular supply, associated lymph nodes, and a sufficient margin of surrounding tissues, especially around a tumor, to ensure that all diseased tissue is removed. Resection: Surgical excision (removal) of tissues, organs, or other structures, in whole or in part. Tracheostomy: A surgical procedure in which the provider makes an incision into the trachea or windpipe, through the neck, and inserts a tube to make an artificial opening to assist breathing; also tracheotomy. Tips For excision of less than one–half of the tongue, see 41120. For a hemiglossectomy (excision of one–half of the tongue), see 41130. For a partial glossectomy with radical neck dissection on only one side of the neck, see 41135. For a complete or total glossectomy, with or without tracheostomy, see 41140 if the procedure is performed without radical neck dissection and 41145 if the procedure includes radical neck dissection. For composite glossectomy with resection of floor of mouth and mandibular resection, without radical neck dissection, see 41150. For composite glossectomy with resection of floor of mouth and suprahyoid neck dissection, see 41153. Read Less

short_description: Palatoplasty for cleft palate, soft and/or hard palate only
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs palatoplasty to correct a cleft palate and close a channel between the oral and nasal cavities. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, which may include placement of an endotracheal tube, the provider begins repair of the soft palate, the hard palate, or both, based on the patient’s specific needs. In a typical procedure, the provider makes an incision in the mucosa of the palate. He raises the mucosal flaps through the incision made. Taking care to protect the endotracheal tube, the provider repairs the abnormal levator muscle by attaching it back to the soft palate. To repair the hard palate, the provider makes an incision in the mucosa of the palate adjacent to the alveolar bone and releases the palatal mucosa from the bony palate. He prepares the edges of the cleft for closure to close the abnormal channel between the oral and nasal cavities. The provider checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision in the soft palate, hard palate, or both with sutures in layers. Terminology Alveolar bone: A thick bone that makes up the bony process of the upper jaw, called the maxilla, and the lower jaw, called the mandible; includes sockets for the teeth; the bone has small blood vessels and a nerve supply, and it provides support to the teeth. Cleft palate: A deformity present from birth in which there is an opening or split in the roof of the mouth, called the palate, in the upper lip, or both; leads to an abnormal communication between the nasal passage and the mouth. Endotracheal tube: A flexible tube inserted into the trachea via the nose or mouth to maintain an open airway. Hard palate: The anterior, or front, portion of the palate that forms the roof of the mouth and separates the oral and the nasal cavities. Hemostasis: Stopping of bleeding from incision or suture lines. Levator muscle: Sling like muscle that helps in lifting the soft palate upward and backward, thereby closing the entry to the nasal cavity. Mucosa: A moist lining of on the inner surface of many body structures, such as the mouth, nose, and lungs. Palatoplasty: Surgical procedure to correct or reconstruct the palate, as in a person with cleft palate, and restore the palate’s function. Soft palate: The back portion of the mouth composed mostly of muscular tissue; also called the velum. Trachea: Respiratory structure composed primarily of muscle and cartilage that connects the pharynx and larynx, or throat and voice box, to the lungs; also called the windpipe. Tips Before choosing your final code for cleft palate palatoplasty, review 42200 to 42225 to be sure you’ve chosen the most appropriate code for your case. Also review 40700 to 40761 for plastic repair of cleft lip or nasal deformity. Read Less

short_description: Palatoplasty for cleft palate, with closure of alveolar ridge; with bone graft to alveolar ridge (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: The provider repairs a cleft palate (palatoplasty) which includes closure of a gap in the alveolar ridge and bone graft to the alveolar ridge. This procedure includes obtaining the bone graft, so do not report that separately. Explanation Cleft palate is a congenital defect that occurs when the palate's median line doesn't fuse together properly during development. With a cleft palate, the main muscle of soft palate (the levator muscle) is abnormally attached to the posterior edge of the hard palate and to the cleft sides. There are numerous techniques for cleft palate repair (palatoplasty), depending on whether the repair is of the hard palate or soft palate, the age of the patient, and whether the repair is performed at a single session or in stages. Techniques are still evolving as there is no one ideal technique. An improperly repaired cleft palate can lead to oral/nasal recommunication, developmental growth restrictions, or velopharyngeal incompetence. With the patient placed supine (face up) with the neck extended, appropriately prepped, and under general anesthesia, the provider inserts an endotracheal (ET) tube through the mouth and places a mouth gag. He injects an epinephrine/saline solution into the area to be operated to constrict the vessels and help minimize bleeding. Depending on the technique employed, the provider corrects the abnormal position of the soft palate muscles, which may involve moving them retrograde (toward the back) and creates a muscle sling. He may create flaps to cover the cleft defect and any raw areas caused by the revision. To repair a defect in the alveolar ridge, the provider takes bone marrow, typically from the patient's hip or tibia (shin bone), to use as a graft. He makes a small incision in the skin over the pelvis. He creates a window in the outer surface (cortex) of the bone and scoops out the inner marrow bone. He closes the graft incision in layers. He then incises the mucosa covering the bone of the gum and peels it away from the gap in the alveolar ridge bone. He creates a pocket in the mucosa on each side and packs the bone marrow into this pocket to fill the entire gap. He closes the gum over the graft of the alveolar bone. He finally closes the remaining defect(s) with tension–free sutures. If the patient has a bifid (split) uvula, he repairs it to a more normal contour and position. He irrigates the operative field and checks for bleeding after which he removes the ET tube and mouth gag. Acquiring the material for the bone graft is included in this procedure; do not report it separately. Terminology Alveolar ridge: A ridgelike border on the upper and lower jaw from where the teeth arise. Cleft palate: Congenital defect in which a cleft (gap) occurs in the palate at its midline, often occurring in conjunction with a cleft lip. Endotracheal tube: A flexible tube inserted into the trachea via the nose or mouth to maintain an open airway. Mucosa: Another name for mucous membrane, the moisture–laden layer of endothelial cells that line the insides of body cavities and the insides of structures that open to the outside of the body, such as the nose, mouth, and rectum. Palatoplasty: A surgical procedure to correct or reconstruct the palate, as in a person with cleft palate, and restore the palate's function. Velopharyngeal incompetence: Improper closure of the velopharyngeal sphincter (muscle of the soft palate), resulting in difficulty in feeding and/or a voice resonance disorder. Tips For other palatoplasty procedures, see 42205 through 42225. For other repair procedures of the palate, see 42226 through 42235. Some of the techniques for palatoplasty that you may see in the documentation include von Langenbeck's bipedicle flap technique, Veau–Wardill–Kilner Pushback technique, Bardach's two–flap technique, Furlow Double opposing Z–Plasty, two–stage palatal repair, hole–in–one repair, raw area free palatoplasty, alveolar extension palatoplasty (AEP), primary pharyngeal flap, intravelar veloplasty, vomer flap, and buccal myomucosal flap. Every surgeon, even if he uses a particular technique, may modify the procedure. Read Less

short_description: Palatoplasty for cleft palate; attachment pharyngeal flap
lay_term: During this procedure, the physician revises previous cleft palate incisions using pharyngeal flap techniques. This procedure is often performed to restore velopharyngeal competence, the functional seal between the nasal cavity and the oral cavity. Explanation The provider performs a revision (repair) of the abnormal separation in the nasal–oral–partition, while fusing pharyngeal flaps to the soft palate. He attaches tissue from the posterior pharyngeal wall to the soft palate. This creates a midline, subtotal obstruction of the oral and nasal cavities with 2 small lateral openings. These remain patent during respiration and nasal consonant production and close for oral consonants. He incises the soft palate in the sagittal midline from the uvula toward the junction of the soft and hard palates. He sutures the flap to the nasal side of the soft palate with interrupted sutures. He partially closes the donor site with sutures. He places nasopharyngeal airways through each lateral pharyngeal port for sizing and postoperative airway support. He then closes the oral side of the soft palate with interrupted sutures. This procedure is often performed to treat velopharyngeal incompetence, the functional seal between the nasal cavity and the oral cavity. Velopharyngeal incompetence: Improper closure of the velopharyngeal sphincter (muscle of the soft palate), resulting in difficulty in feeding and/or a voice resonance disorder. short_description: Excision of parotid tumor or parotid gland; lateral lobe, with dissection and preservation of facial nerve
lay_term: The provider excises the lateral lobe of a parotid tumor or the parotid glad with dissection and preservation of the facial nerve. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a preauricular curvilinear incision and extends it horizontally to the neck. The provider dissects the skin further and uses a nerve stimulator to identify the facial nerve. She identifies the lateral lobe of the gland or any neoplastic growth in the parotid's lateral lobe and removes it while preserving the integrity of the entire facial nerve. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision in layers. Tips Most payers do not pay for neuro monitoring during this procedure, even when it is done by another provider. To bill for neuro monitoring, make sure the diagnosis used is the diagnosis documented. If a payer has a limitation on the diagnoses and pays for the monitoring, the diagnoses will be specific to the payer. This means you need to indicate what is documented. short_description: Excision of parotid tumor or parotid gland; total, with dissection and preservation of facial nerve
lay_term: The provider removes a parotid gland with a tumor and performs dissection and preservation of the facial nerve. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a curvilinear incision in front of the ear with a sharp instrument. He extends the incision to the neck toward the mid jaw bone. He further dissects the tissue and then uses an electrical nerve stimulation device to locate and preserve the integrity of the facial nerve during the procedure. He dissects the lateral lobe from the nerve branches. He moves the nerve to protect it during removal of the rest of the gland. He closes the incision in layers. Terminology Parotid gland: Salivary gland situated on each side of the face below and in front of the ear. short_description: Parotid duct diversion, bilateral (Wilke type procedure)
lay_term: The provider performs a Wilke type procedure, or parotid duct rerouting, typically to treat sialorrhea (drooling). Explanation The patient is given preoperative antibiotics and dexamethasone. The patient is placed supine (face up) on the operating table. With the patient appropriately prepped and under general anesthesia, the provider sterilizes the oral cavity, places teeth blocks to keep the mouth open, and places a throat pack to block the throat. He grasps the tongue with a retractor and moves it out of the field of dissection. He identifies the opening of a parotid duct and cannulates it with a lacrimal probe. He infiltrates the mucosa surrounding the opening with epinephrine and lidocaine to help control bleeding and incises the mucosa once vasoconstriction is evident. He dissects out the parotid duct and relocates it via a submucosal tunnel into the anterior tonsillar pillar (a fold of tissue in front of the tonsil) using autologous vein grafts. He repeats the procedure on the opposite side. When the procedure is complete, the provider removes all instruments and packs from the surgical field. This procedure is typically performed to treat excessive drooling. Terminology Cannulate or cannulize: To introduce or insert a cannula, a tube less flexible than a catheter, into a body cavity or duct through which other instruments can be inserted, medicines administered, or fluid drained. Epinephrine: An injectable blood vessel constricting and antiallergic medication. Mucosa: Another name for mucous membrane, the moisture–laden layer of endothelial cells that line the insides of body cavities and the insides of structures that open to the outside of the body, such as the nose, mouth, and rectum. Parotid gland: One of a pair of saliva–secreting glands present in front of and below the ear on each side; the largest of all the salivary glands. Probe: (Verb) To explore a wound or the inside of a vessel, organ, or the body such as with a blunt–tipped surgical instrument; (noun) a blunt–tipped surgical instrument. Secondary intention healing: Healing process in which a wound is left to heal on its own. Sialorrhea: Also known as drooling; excessive increase or production of saliva which flows out of the mouth Submandibular gland: Salivary gland inside of and near the lower edge of the mandible on each side; also known as the submaxillary gland. Tonsils: A pair of lymphoid masses located on each side of the throat. Tips This is a bilateral procedure, so do NOT add modifier 50 when you report this code. Since there is no code for parotid duct rerouting with excision or ligation of only one submandibular gland, you may be able to report this code with modifier 22 if only one submandibular gland was excised or ligated. To avoid denials and resubmissions, check with the payer first. For the same procedure with excision of both submandibular glands, see 42509. For the same procedure with ligation of both submandibular glands, see 42510. It is usually a good idea to get prior approval for procedures like this because the procedure may be covered for certain indications but not for others. Check with the payer to ascertain whether or not the procedure will be covered, and of course, the patient should be made aware if the procedure is not covered. Additional Info Sialorrhea (excessive drooling) is a common problem in children with mental retardation or cerebral palsy and adults with Parkinson's disease or who have had a stroke. Read Less

short_description: Radical resection of tonsil, tonsillar pillars, and/or retromolar trigone; without closure
lay_term: The provider removes the tonsils, tonsillar pillars and/or the retromolar trigone (the small area behind the wisdom teeth). If necessary, he also removes portions of the maxilla or mandible that are affected. The resulting wound is so large that it is left open to be grafted during a later procedure. This procedure is often used to remove cancerous growths. Explanation With the patient under anesthesia, the physician makes an incision at the neck region and removes the tonsils, tonsillar pillars, and/or the retromolar trigone. He may also remove nearby structures (e.g., lymph nodes) as needed. If necessary, he also removes portions of the maxilla or mandible that are affected. The resulting wound is so large that it is left open to be grafted during a later procedure. This procedure is often used to remove cancerous growths. Terminology Radical resection (or dissection): Surgical removal of a structure to include its vascular supply, associated lymph nodes, and a sufficient margin of surrounding tissues, especially around a tumor; describes any extensive surgery to ensure that all diseased tissue is removed. Retromolar trigone: The small area behind the wisdom teeth. Tonsils: A pair of lymphoid masses located on each side of the throat. Tips For the same procedure but with closure with a local tongue or buccal flap, report 42844, and for the same procedure with closure with a local flap other than tongue or buccal, report 42845. short_description: Control oropharyngeal hemorrhage, primary or secondary (eg, post-tonsillectomy); simple
lay_term: The provider control bleeding in the mouth and throat within 24 hours (primary) or from 24 hours up to two weeks (secondary), after a surgical procedure such as a tonsillectomy; the procedure is uncomplicated and does not require hospital admission. Explanation The patient continues to bleed or rebleeds following a prior surgical procedure, such as a tonsillectomy. Following application of local anesthesia, the provider controls bleeding in the mouth and throat using simple techniques like bipolar electrocautery (using high–frequency electric current to cauterize lesions or to stop bleeding by burning the tissue) or hot water irrigation with saline (salt water). Once hemostasis (control of bleeding) is assured and the patient has recovered, he discharges the patient from the outpatient facility. Terminology Electrocautery: Control of bleeding or sealing or destruction of other tissues using high–frequency electrical current; also called electric coagulation or electrocoagulation. Hemorrhage: Bleeding; typically refers to uncontrolled, rapid and/or excessive bleeding. Oropharynx: The portion of the throat (pharynx) that is open to the mouth; includes the base of the tongue, tonsils, and soft palate. Tonsils: A pair of lymphoid masses located on each side of the throat. Tips For the same procedure requiring hospitalization because closure is more complicated, see 42961. For control of bleeding requiring surgical intervention, see 42962. For control of post–op nasopharyngeal bleeding, such as after an adenoidectomy, see 42970 to 42972. Each of these codes crosses to anesthesia code 00170, Anesthesia for intraoral procedures, including biopsy; not otherwise specified. Because Medicare bundles all care of post–operative complications that do not require a return to the operating room into the original procedure, you should not report 42960 for control of post–op oropharyngeal bleeding or 42970 for control of post–op nasopharyngeal bleeding for Medicare payers. These are simple procedures, usually performed in the surgeon's office (and therefore not generally billed in an ASC in the first place). Although the descriptors for codes 42960 to 42962 give the example of post–tonsillectomy bleeding and 42970 to 42972 suggests post–adenoidectomy bleeding, all these codes represent control of the hemorrhage by location and can, therefore, be used to report control of bleeding in these areas following other types of procedures, such as surgery for resection of cancer. The parenthetical references in the descriptors are merely examples and do not exclude other causes of bleeding in the areas defined by the descriptors. The abbreviation e.g. in (e.g., post–tonsillectomy) and (e.g., post adenoidectomy) is for the Latin exempli gratia, "for example." If the complication occurs during the global period of the original procedure and the otolaryngologist had to return the patient to the operating room, you should append modifier 78 (Return to the operating room for a related procedure during the postoperative period) to 42962 and 42972. Without the modifier, the insurer may bundle 42962 into the procedures global period. Be sure to link 42962 to 42972 to the hemorrhage complication through the diagnosis code you select, not to the reason for the original surgery. Read Less

short_description: Drug-induced sleep endoscopy, with dynamic evaluation of velum, pharynx, tongue base, and larynx for evaluation of sleep-disordered breathing, flexible, diagnostic Notes: (Do not report 42975 in conjunction with 31231, unless performed for a separate condition [ie, other than sleep-disordered breathing] and using a separate endoscope) (Do not report 42975 in conjunction with 31575, 92511)
lay_term: After the patient receives sedation and is asleep, the provider uses an endoscope to assess the throat and check the palate and tongue areas. The goal is to determine where airway obstruction is occurring in a patient with sleep–disordered breathing, such as obstructive sleep apnea, to determine the best treatment. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a flexible endoscope (a tubular instrument with a light source and camera) into the patient’s airway, such as through one side of the nose. This may occur as the patient begins to snore and have breathing blockage. The provider evaluates the throat and observes the palate and tongue regions to check where blockage is occurring. The provider checks the velum (soft palate), pharynx (cavity behind the nose and mouth), tongue base, and larynx (hollow area that holds the vocal cords and leads to the lungs). Determining where blockage is occurring helps the provider determine which treatments will have the best outcomes for the patient’s sleep–disordered breathing, such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). OSA is a condition occurring during sleep in which breathing stops intermittently for brief periods, disrupting the sleep cycle and resulting in daytime sleepiness; it is caused by obstruction, narrowing, or incompetence of the airway. The provider then removes the scope to complete the procedure. Read Less

short_description: Total or near total esophagectomy, without thoracotomy; with pharyngogastrostomy or cervical esophagogastrostomy, with or without pyloroplasty (transhiatal)
lay_term: The provider performs removal of all or most of the esophagus and then connects the stomach to the pharynx or the cervical esophagus. He may widen the opening at the bottom of the stomach. He does not use a chest incision for the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the neck just above the collarbone and cuts the esophagus free of its supports. He divides the esophagus. If he can save part of the esophagus, he makes the division in the neck. If he can save none of the esophagus, he divides it higher up where it begins at the pharynx. He then makes an incision in the upper abdomen just below the diaphragm. This procedure is transhiatal, which refers to through the esophageal hiatus, the opening the esophagus goes through in the diaphragm. He enters the abdomen and visualizes the stomach and gastro esophageal, or GE, junction where the stomach and esophagus meet. He then divides the esophagus from the stomach and removes the esophagus through the abdominal wound. He pulls the stomach up into the chest and connects the stomach to the remaining cervical esophagus or to the pharynx. The provider may surgically alter the stomach to allow food to pass more easily through the stomach. This procedure is called pyloroplasty and involves using incisions to widen the pylorus, the valve structure between the stomach and small intestine. The provider may use air or dye to check for leaks at the anastomotic sites. He inspects both wounds and closes the incisions in layers. The provider typically performs this procedure to remove cancer of the esophagus, to remove areas of the esophagus that have been badly damaged by ingestion of caustic fluids, or to repair spontaneous ruptures of the esophagus. Terminology Cervical esophagogastrostomy: Connection of the cervical esophagus, the portion in the neck, to the stomach. Diaphragm: Membrane dividing the abdominal and chest, or thoracic, cavities. Esophagectomy: Surgical removal of a part or the entire esophagus. Esophagus: Muscular tube that carries substances from the pharynx, which is behind the mouth, down to the stomach. Pharyngogastrostomy: Connection of the pharynx to the stomach. Pharynx: Area of the throat where the nose passages connect to the trachea, or windpipe, and the esophagus, which is the tube to the stomach. Pyloroplasty: Surgery to widen the opening in the lower part of the stomach so that stomach contents can empty into the small intestine. Thoracotomy: Surgical incision of the chest. Tips Use 43112 when the service involves removal of most or all of the esophagus and attachment of the stomach to the pharynx or cervical esophagus with thoracotomy i.e., McKeown esophagectomy or tri–incisional esophagectomy. The provider may or may not perform pyloroplasty. There are numerous esophagectomy procedure codes. For other total or near–total esophagectomy procedures, see 43107–43113 and 43286–43288; for partial esophagectomy procedures, see 43116–43123, and for total or partial esophagectomy without reconstruction, see 43124. short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical, esophagomyotomy (Heller type), with fundoplasty, when performed Notes: (For open approach, see 43330, 43331) (Do not report 43279 in conjunction with 43280)
lay_term: The provider performs laparoscopic esophagomyotomy, cutting an esophageal muscle, and may or may not perform fundoplasty, wrapping part of the stomach around the esophagus. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision at the umbilicus, or navel, and uses this opening to insufflate, or blow gas into, the abdomen. This insufflation will lift the abdominal wall away from the organs and will improve visualization of the site to be treated. He then makes additional small incisions and inserts a camera and instruments to perform the procedure. He then enters the abdomen and removes any adhesions present. He may use suction to evacuate blood and clots from the abdomen to improve visibility prior to beginning the Heller type procedure. He identifies the esophagus and stomach. He then makes incisions through the superficial layers of the esophagus, lower esophageal sphincter, and stomach, leaving the inner layer intact. If he chooses to perform fundoplasty, he then wraps a flap from the stomach around the distal esophagus, causing the sphincter to close when the stomach contracts, limiting reflux. The provider assures hemostasis. He then closes the abdominal incision in layers. The provider may choose this procedure as surgical treatment for esophageal achalasia. The treatment allows the esophageal sphincter to relax properly and allows food to pass into the stomach. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands that form between tissues and organs, sometimes as a result of injury during surgery; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Esophageal achalasia: Failure of the esophageal sphincter to relax and the esophageal muscles to propel food, making swallowing and the passage of food into the stomach difficult. Esophagomyotomy: Incision through the musculature of the esophagus. Esophagus: Muscular tube that carries substances from the pharynx, which is behind the mouth, down to the stomach. Fundoplication, fundoplasty: Wrapping of the gastric fundus, that part of the stomach that rises above the point where the esophagus opens into the stomach, around the esophagus for the treatment of gastroesophageal reflux; fundoplication techniques include Nissen and Toupet. Hemostasis: Stopping of bleeding from incisions and suture lines. Laparoscopy: The provider typically makes several incisions in the abdomen, inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure, inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen, and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments; he places devices called ports to keep the incisions open, removes the ports at the conclusion of the procedure, and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. lay_term: The provider implants a magnetic band around the junction of the esophagus and stomach to narrow the opening and prevent the backflow of stomach contents, known as gastroesophageal reflux (GER), using a laparoscopic approach. The provider may also perform a cruroplasty to strengthen the diaphragm and prevent a hiatal hernia. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision at the umbilicus, or navel, and uses this opening to insufflate, or blow gas into, the abdomen, which lifts the abdominal wall away from the organs and improves visualization of the site to be treated. He makes additional small incisions and inserts a camera and instruments to perform the procedure. Once he enters the abdomen and has good visualization of the cavity, he implants a sphincter augmentation device at the gastroesophageal junction. The device consists of a stainless steel cable connecting multiple magnetic beads. These beads surround the sphincter, and their magnetic force closes the sphincter when exposed to stomach acid, and remains open while eating and drinking. Esophagus: Muscular tube that carries substances from the pharynx, which is behind the mouth, down to the stomach. Gastroesophageal junction: The point at which the esophagus enters the stomach where there is a visible change in the lining, or epithelium, of the esophagus; also known as the esophagogastric junction, or EG junction. Hiatal hernia: Bulging of an organ through a weakness in the diaphragmatic wall where the esophagus passes through. short_description: Esophagectomy, total or near total, with laparoscopic mobilization of the abdominal and mediastinal esophagus and proximal gastrectomy, with laparoscopic pyloric drainage procedure if performed, with open cervical pharyngogastrostomy or esophagogastrostomy (ie, laparoscopic transhiatal esophagectomy)
lay_term: The provider removes all or most of the esophagus, removes the upper part of the stomach, and frees up (mobilizes) the part of the esophagus behind the mediastinum (if that part remains) using laparoscopic access; he then uses an open cervical approach to connect the stomach to the pharynx (pharyngogastrostomy) or to the remnant of the esophagus (esophagogastrostomy). He may or may not perform a pyloric drainage procedure during the laparoscopic portion of the procedure. Explanation After appropriate preparation and under general anesthesia, the patient is placed in a supine position. The provider makes several small incisions in the abdomen and subcoastal region of the left and right midclavicular line through which trocars (tubelike devices with pointed ends) are inserted. One of the trocars is used to introduce the laparoscope while the others are used to insert surgical instruments. Once he enters the abdomen and has good visualization of the area, he takes down any adhesions. He then identifies the esophagus and divides it proximally from the pharynx and distally from the stomach in the following manner. If he can save part of the esophagus, he makes the division in the neck. If he can save none of the esophagus, he divides it higher up where it begins at the pharynx. He then inserts a camera and instruments in the abdominal incision and enters the abdomen and visualizes the stomach and gastroesophageal (GE) junction where the stomach and esophagus meet. He then divides the esophagus from the stomach and removes the esophagus and the proximal part of the stomach. The provider may decide to operate on the pyloric valve to improve the flow of food from the stomach to the intestines. This procedure is called pyloroplasty and involves using incisions to widen the pylorus, the valve structure between the stomach and small intestine. The provider may use air or dye to check for leaks. He inspects the area for bleeding and removes the instruments and scope and closes the laparoscopic incisions in layers. The provider makes an incision in the upper chest/neck area and pulls the stomach up. He connects the proximal end of the stomach to the remnant of the esophagus or, in the case of total esophagectomy, to the pharynx. He checks the anastomosis for leaks and checks again for bleeding, then closes the incision. short_description: Esophagomyotomy (Heller type); abdominal approach Notes: (For laparoscopic esophagomyotomy procedure, use 43279)

short_description: Esophagojejunostomy (without total gastrectomy); abdominal approach

short_description: Gastrointestinal reconstruction for previous esophagectomy, for obstructing esophageal lesion or fistula, or for previous esophageal exclusion; with colon interposition or small intestine reconstruction, including intestine mobilization, preparation, and anastomosis(es)
lay_term: The provider reoperates on a patient who had previous removal of all or part of the esophagus. He excises more diseased tissue or scar tissue, dilates, or widens, narrowed segments of the previous repair, or reconstructs the remaining anatomy. He performs the procedure to relieve obstructions and enable the patient to swallow properly. Explanation With the patient lying supine on the operating table and after the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes one or two incisions, opening the chest and abdomen. He examines the esophageal remnant and identifies the site of any obstruction or disease. If he deems it appropriate, he excises obstructing tissue or dilates the narrowed obstructed area and repairs the esophagus. If he feels a graft is necessary, the provider identifies and harvests a section of colon or small bowel. He anastomoses, or reconnects, the remaining ends of the bowel end to end. He sutures the removed portion of bowel proximally to the esophageal stump and distally to the stomach. The provider may also decide to dilate, or widen, the distal stomach to allow for easier passage of food. The provider assures hemostasis, removes all instruments, and closes the abdominal and chest incisions in layers. short_description: Gastrectomy, total; with esophagoenterostomy
lay_term: The provider creates a surgical opening between the esophagus and intestine following excision of the stomach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an upper left paramedian incision. He mobilizes the spleen with its hilar lymph nodes, splenic vessels, and the tail and the body of the pancreas from left to the right. He performs a retroperitoneal procedure, working behind the peritoneum. He resects the stomach with both lesser and greater omentum and lymph nodes around the celiac axis. He ligates the left gastric, right gastric, and epiploic arteries. After excision of the whole stomach, he closes the cut edge of the pancreas with sutures. He maintains the continuity of the alimentary canal with an esophagoenterostomy, a connection between the esophagus and intestine. He inserts a drain up to the pancreas and brings the other end out through a separate stab incision at the subcostal region. He closes the incision. Terminology Omentum: Double fold of peritoneum attached to stomach. Retroperitoneal: Behind and outside the peritoneum. Tips For a partial gastrectomy, also known as a hemigastrectomy, select the appropriate code from the range 43632 to 43634, Excision Procedures on the Stomach, depending upon which portion of the stomach the provider removes. short_description: Gastrectomy, total; with formation of intestinal pouch, any type
lay_term: The provider removes the entire stomach and creates a pouch between the esophagus and duodenum to maintain an uninterrupted digestive tract. He typically performs this procedure in patients with cancer of the stomach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an upper left paramedian incision in the abdomen. He frees up the spleen with its attachments and also the pancreas. He excises the stomach with both lesser and greater omentum and surrounding lymph nodes. He ligates or ties off the arteries feeding the stomach. After removing the stomach from the field, he repairs the cut surface of the pancreas. He then creates a pouch between the esophagus and duodenum to, in essence, replace the stomach. He chooses from several techniques to create the pouch. For example, if he chooses to anastomose a loop of jejunum side to side to the esophagus and to the duodenum, he frees up the jejunum from its attachments. Then, he makes a cut in the side of the jejunum in two places, suturing one opening side to side to the esophagus and one to the duodenum so that food will pass through the pouch and provide for greater absorption of nutrients. He also anastomoses the cut ends of the esophagus and duodenum to each other. This restores an uninterrupted digestive tract. Before closure he places a drain in the abdominal cavity up to pancreas and brings the other end out through a separate stab incision at the subcostal region. The provider then checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Absorption: Taking in of substances by tissues. Anastomosis: Connection between two structures, anatomical or surgically created, such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end to side and side to side. Diagnostic: Refers to procedures performed for the purpose of determining the type of disease and its causes. Duodenum: First part of the small intestine. Esophagus: The muscular tube that carries substances from the pharynx, which is behind the mouth, down to the stomach. Gastrectomy: Partial or total excision of the stomach. Intestinal pouch: The creation of a pouch within the digestive tract to replace the stomach after total gastrectomy. Jejunum: Second part of the small intestine. Lymph node: A knot or swelling at various spots along the circulation of the lymph system; the lymph system maintains fluid balance by returning fluid from the spaces between tissues back to the blood stream and supports the immune system. Nutrient: Food or other substance that provides the body with energy and sustains life and health. Omentum: Part of the membrane lining the abdominal cavity that extends from the stomach to the adjacent organs. Pancreas: An organ situated between the spleen and duodenum; it produces insulin and enzymes that aid in the digestion of protein. Therapeutic: For treatment purposes. Paramedian: Just to the side of midline. Spleen: An organ in the abdomen near the stomach; it produces and destroys red blood cells and supports the immune system. Read Less

short_description: Gastrectomy, partial, distal; with gastroduodenostomy
lay_term: The provider excises the diseased portion of the stomach and reconnects the remnant of the stomach to the duodenum to maintain an uninterrupted digestive tract. He typically performs this procedure in patients with cancer of the stomach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the abdomen, typically from the point at the lower end of the sternum to the umbilicus. He places retractors to hold the incision open and allow for exploration of the abdomen. He frees up the stomach and the first part of the duodenum by cutting through the peritoneum over the duodenum. He divides the duodenum between clamps, just inferior to or below, the pylorus. He covers the lower cut end of the duodenum with gauze and keeps it aside for further anastomosis. He anastomoses, or joins, the cut ends of the stomach and the duodenum without any tension between them. He may place a tube in the abdomen and bring it out through a separate stab wound for drainage. The provider then checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision in the abdomen. Terminology Duodenum: First part of the small intestine. Gastrectomy: Partial or total excision of the stomach. Gastroduodenostomy: A created opening, or anastomosis, between the stomach and duodenum. Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Pylorus: A circular band of muscular tissue at the base of the stomach; it acts like a sphincter controlling the passage of stomach contents into the duodenum. Retractor: Surgical instrument used to retract, or hold back, wound edges or deeper tissues to give better visualization and access to the provider performing surgery. Tips Code 43631 describes the surgical removal of part of the stomach; i.e., excision of the pylorus of the stomach with the anastomosis of the upper portion of the stomach to the duodenum. For the gastroduodenostomy portion of the procedure, check the operative note for indications that the provider creates a surgical passageway between the stomach and the duodenum. During a gastrectomy, the provider may perform additional procedures, such as a vagotomy, the surgical cutting of the vagus nerve to reduce acid secretion in the stomach. The global period for 43631 is 90 days. Because 43635, Vagotomy when performed with partial distal gastrectomy, list separately in addition to codes for a primary procedure, is an add–on code with a ZZZ global period, all components of the global surgical package related to 43635 are included in the 90–day global period of its parent code, 43631. short_description: Gastrectomy, partial, distal; with gastrojejunostomy
lay_term: The provider excises the diseased portion of the stomach and reconnects the remnant of the stomach to the jejunum to maintain an uninterrupted digestive tract. He typically performs this procedure in patients with cancer of the stomach. Explanation The provider gains access through a right upper paramedian incision, opening the peritoneum to one or the other side of the falciform ligament. He examines the stomach and duodenum to know the exact details of the pathology. He draws the stomach out of the wound and estimates the probable extent of resection. He detaches the greater omentum from the stomach by division between successive pairs of artery forceps applied close to the greater curvature of the stomach. Then he detaches the lesser omentum from the lesser curvature. He holds the stomach up with clamps so that the left gastric vessels are tensed. He carefully clamps, dissects, and ligates the vessels. He selects a line for division of the stomach to remove the distal half. He trims loose tissues just above the proposed line of transection off from the greater and lesser curvatures. He splits the transverse mesocolon vertically through an avascular area to enter the lesser sac. He draws the posterior wall of the stomach out through the split in the mesocolon and applies Allis tissue forceps to the fold. He applies a pair of occlusion clamps so that bleeding or secretions do not disturb the anastomosis. He passes a hand along the undersurface of the transverse mesocolon, just below the tail of the pancreas, where the duodenojejunal flexure is found, and the first loop of jejunum is situated here. He picks it up and places it by the side of the posterior wall of stomach so the proximal part of jejunum lies near the lesser curvature and the distal part near the greater curvature, and thus an isoperistaltic anastomosis is formed. He closes the opening of the transverse mesocolon, checks that the closure is secure, checks for bleeding, and closes the abdominal incision. Terminology Duodenum: The first part of the small intestine. Falciform ligament: The ligament that divides the liver into two lobes and attaches it to the front wall of the abdomen. Flexure: A curved or bent part of an organ or other structure, e.g., hepatic flexure, sigmoid flexure, splenic flexure. Greater curvature of the stomach: The outer lateral margin of the stomach that forms the bulk of the stomach. Jejunum: Second part of the small intestine. Lesser curvature of the stomach: One part of the stomach, the inner inferior margin of the stomach, beginning where the esophagus enters the stomach and ending where the pylorus empties into the duodenum. Mesocolon: A membrane joining the colon to the posterior abdominal wall. Omentum: Part of the membrane lining the abdominal cavity that extends from the stomach to the adjacent organs. Pancreas: An organ in the abdomen that produces enzymes to aid in digestion and control of blood sugar; islets cells scattered through the pancreas secrete a variety of hormones, including glucagon and insulin.. Paramedian incision: An incision lateral to or just to the side of the midline. Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Tips The distal partial gastrectomy code series is broken down in roughly the same manner as the total gastrectomy series: 43631 (Gastrectomy, partial, distal; with gastroduodenostomy), 43632 (… with gastrojejunostomy), 43633 (… with Roux–en–Y reconstruction) and 43634 (… with the formation of intestinal pouch). short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical, gastric restrictive procedure; with gastric bypass and Roux-en-Y gastroenterostomy (roux limb 150 cm or less) Notes: (Do not report 43644 in conjunction with 43846, 49320) (Esophagogastroduodenoscopy [EGD] performed for a separate condition should be reported with modifier 59) (For greater than 150 cm, use 43645) (For open procedure, use 43846)
lay_term: The provider surgically reduces the size of the stomach by bypassing a portion of it and creates a connection between the stomach and the jejunum via laparoscopic technique to treat morbid obesity. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes several laparoscopic incisions and inserts a scope and surgical instruments. He inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure. The provider divides the small bowel below the lower stomach outlet and rearranges it into Y formation so that the food flows out from the small upper stomach pouch into a Roux limb. Alternatively, the provider places the Y intersection near the upper, or proximal, end of the small bowel. Then the provider constructs the Roux limb, preserving most of the small bowel for absorption of nutrients. The provider then checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision in the abdomen. Terminology Absorption: Taking in of substances by tissues. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD): A procedure that involves passing a lighted scope through the mouth and down through the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum; the procedure may be performed for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes. Gastric bypass: A surgical procedure that reroutes the digestive tract past the stomach, essentially walling off the stomach from the digestive tract without removing it. Gastric restrictive procedure: A surgical procedure that employs various techniques to reduce the size of the stomach. Jejunum: Second part of the small intestine. Laparoscopy: The provider typically makes several incisions in the abdomen, inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure, inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen, and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments; he places devices called ports to keep the incisions open, removes the ports and deflates the abdomen at the conclusion of the procedure, and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. Morbid obesity: So overweight that it endangers health; although definitions vary, typical values for determining morbid obesity include a body mass index, a method for determining body fat, equal to or greater than 40 or being 100 pounds, or 45 kg, overweight. Nutrient: Food or other substance that provides the body with energy and sustains life and health. Roux–en–Y gastroenterostomy: A surgical procedure that involves anastomosing the stomach to the jejunum; the procedure helps prevent gastric reflux in patients who undergo gastric bypass procedures. Tips Operative procedures for morbid obesity may not be covered by Medicare or other payers; check with the payer to determine coverage. For laparoscopic gastric bypass and small intestine reconstruction to limit absorption or for a roux limb greater than 150 cm, see 43645. For the same procedure, but using an open technique, see 43846, and for open gastric bypass with small intestine reconstruction to limit absorption or for a roux limb greater than 150 cm, see 43847. For a vertical–banded gastroplasty for morbid obesity, see 43842, and for a gastric restrictive procedure other than vertical–banded gastroplasty without gastric bypass, see 43843. See 43775 for laparoscopic longitudinal gastrectomy or sleeve gastrectomy, and 43770 for laparoscopic placement of an adjustable gastric restrictive device. Read Less

short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical, gastric restrictive procedure; with gastric bypass and small intestine reconstruction to limit absorption Notes: (Do not report 43645 in conjunction with 49320, 43847)
lay_term: The provider creates a small gastric reservoir using the upper portion of the stomach and connects it to the small intestine. In doing so, he bypasses the main body of the stomach, effectively restricting the amount of food a patient can consume at one time and also limiting absorption. He performs the procedure to treat morbid obesity. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and either under monitored anesthesia care (MAC), general anesthesia, or conscious sedation, the provider makes a small incision in the belly button or lower abdomen and fills the abdominal cavity with carbon dioxide in order to lift the abdominal wall away from the internal organs. Then, he inserts a laparoscope through the belly button. The video camera permits the provider to see inside the abdominal area on video monitors located in the operating room. It also allows the provider to take pictures of any problem areas he discovers. Typically, he staples across a portion of the upper stomach to create about a one–ounce reservoir and close off the remaining body of the stomach. He then connects the reservoir to the small intestine, forming a detour for the passage of food around the main body of the stomach. In this procedure, the site of the anastomosis is lower on the small intestine than the Roux en Y, giving the patient a shorter length of intestine for absorption. The provider then checks for bleeding, deflates the abdomen, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incisions in the abdomen. Terminology Endoscope: A stiff or flexible tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source to examine the interior structures of a body cavity such as colon, bladder, or stomach; other instruments can be passed through the channel of the scope. Gastric: Pertaining to the stomach. Gastric bypass and small intestine reconstruction: A surgically created channel, typically from a small remnant of the stomach at the top of the stomach to the duodenum, to exclude the bulk of the stomach from the intestinal tract; also Roux en Y procedure. Gastric restrictive procedure: A surgical procedure that employs various techniques to reduce the size of the stomach. Laparoscopy: The provider typically makes several incisions in the abdomen, inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure, inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen, and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments; he places devices called ports to keep the incisions open, removes the ports and deflates the abdomen at the conclusion of the procedure, and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. Monitored anesthesia care (MAC): A combination of a local anesthetic with sedation, generally administered by a provider who is qualified to provide general anesthesia. Morbid obesity: So overweight that it endangers health; although definitions vary, typical values for determining morbid obesity include a body mass index, a method for determining body fat, equal to or greater than 40 or being 100 pounds, or 45 kg, overweight. Reservoir: A created space for storage; it may be a replacement for an anatomical cavity like the stomach or an artificial container for storage of medicine. Tips Operative procedures for morbid obesity may not be covered by Medicare or other payers; check with the payer to determine coverage. For laparoscopic Roux–en–Y with a roux limb of 150 cm or less for morbid obesity, see 43644. For the same procedure, but using an open technique, see 43846, and for open gastric bypass with small intestine reconstruction to limit absorption or for a roux limb greater than 150 cm, see 43847. For a vertical–banded gastroplasty for morbid obesity, see 43842, and for a gastric restrictive procedure other than vertical–banded gastroplasty without gastric bypass, see 43843. short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical; revision or removal of gastric neurostimulator electrodes, antrum Notes: (For open approach, see 43881, 43882) (For insertion of gastric neurostimulator pulse generator, use 64590) (For revision or removal of gastric neurostimulator pulse generator, use 64595) (For electronic analysis and programming of gastric neurostimulator pulse generator, see 95980, 95981, 95982) (For laparoscopic implantation, revision, or removal of gastric neurostimulator electrodes, lesser curvature [morbid obesity], use 43659)
lay_term: Using laparoscopic technique, the provider tests and adjusts previously placed gastric neurostimulator electrodes or removes them if they do not function as required. Gastric neurostimulators stimulate gastric emptying by activating the muscles around the pylorus. Gastroparesis, or paralysis of the stomach, is often a complication of diabetes mellitus. Explanation With the patient supine on the operating table and after the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision at the umbilicus and uses this opening to inflate the abdomen with carbon dioxide gas. This lifts the abdominal wall away from the organs and improves visibility of the site to be treated. The provider makes additional small incisions and inserts a camera and instruments. Once he enters the abdomen, the provider examines the abdominal cavity. He takes down any adhesions. The gastric neurostimulator is identified and repositioned after he tests it to see if it is working properly and makes any adjustments necessary. If he thinks it necessary, he removes the electrode and the pulse generator from the pocket below the abdominal skin. If an infection is present, he irrigates the area with an antibiotic solution. The provider assures hemostasis. He deflates the abdomen, removes all instruments, and closes the small abdominal incisions in layers. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands that form between tissues and organs, often as a result of injury during surgery; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Antrum: Part of the pyloric channel at the base of the stomach. Electrode: A device used to transmit electrical impulses. Gastric electrical stimulator, GES, or gastric pacemaker: A programmable device similar to a pacemaker for the heart except that the stimulating electrodes are placed on the muscle at the base of the stomach to cause the muscles to contract, restoring function to the pylorus. Gastric: Pertaining to the stomach. Hemostasis: Stopping of bleeding from incisions and suture lines. Laparoscopy: The provider typically makes several incisions in the abdomen, inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure, inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen, and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments; he places devices called ports to keep the incisions open, removes the ports at the conclusion of the procedure, and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. Neurostimulator: A device that uses electrical impulses to activate muscle contraction. Pulse generator: A programmable device that emits electrical pulses; also gastric electrical stimulator or gastric pacemaker. Tips This cutting edge treatment, gastric electrostimulation (GES) has two codes for laparoscopic technique; compare 43647, implantation or replacement, with 43648, Laparoscopy, surgical; revision or removal of gastric neurostimulator electrodes, antrum. Another duo covers the same procedures using an open approach, 43881 for implantation or replacement of gastric neurostimulator electrodes on the antrum and 43882 for revision or removal of gastric neurostimulator electrodes from the antrum. A gastric neurostimulator is approved to treat gastroparesis due to diabetic or idiopathic causes in a patient unresponsive to drug therapy and experiencing severe nutritional deficits; it is not approved for weight loss. short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical; transection of vagus nerves, truncal
lay_term: Using laparoscopic technique, the provider transects both main trunks of the vagus nerve to treat a duodenal ulcer. Explanation When the patient is prepped and under appropriate anesthesia, the provider makes several small incisions in the abdomen and inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide (CO2) for better exposure. He inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen, and places devices called ports in the other incisions to keep them open. He inserts instruments through the other incisions. The provider packs the spleen away with a pack and mobilizes the liver. He retracts the upper part of the stomach downward, opens the visceral peritoneum over the esophagus, and mobilizes the esophagus. He frees up, ligates, and divides the main trunks of the anterior and posterior vagus nerves. He protects the hepatic and celiac branches of the vagus nerves. He controls any bleeding, removes packs and instruments, removes the ports, and closes the laparoscopy incisions. Terminology Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Esophagus: The long tubular portion of the digestive tract that stretches between the throat and the stomach. Pylorus: A circular band of muscular tissue at the base of the stomach; it acts like a sphincter controlling the passage of the stomach contents into the duodenum; the first part of the small intestine. Vagus nerve: Cranial nerve X, one of the twelve nerves of the brain that emerge from the lower portion of the brain (cranial nerves); it is the longest cranial nerve and is involved in sensory and motor function of the respiratory and digestive system as well as the heart. Tips For laparoscopic selective or highly selective surgical transection of the vagus nerve, see 43652. Read Less

short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical; transection of vagus nerves, selective or highly selective
lay_term: The provider uses laparoscopic technique to perform a selective (division of the anterior and posterior gastric nerves of Latarjet only) or highly selective vagotomy (denervation of only the stomach fundus and body, the parietal cell–containing areas). Explanation When the patient is prepped and under appropriate anesthesia, the provider makes several small incisions in the abdomen and inflates the abdomen for better exposure. He inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen, and places devices called ports in the other incisions to keep them open. He inserts instruments through the other incisions. The provider packs the spleen away with a pack and mobilizes the liver. He retracts the upper part of the stomach downward, opens the visceral peritoneum over the esophagus, and mobilizes the esophagus. He frees up, ligates, and divides the anterior and posterior vagus nerves. He protects the hepatic and celiac branches of the vagus nerve. For selective vagotomy, the provider divides the anterior and posterior gastric nerves of Latarjet, which run along the lesser curvature and supply the antrum and pylorus. This denervates the pylorus and the antrum. For highly selective vagotomy the provider divides multiple smaller branches of the vagus nerves of the esophagus and the cardia, fundus, and body of the stomach close to the organs and preserves the main trunk of the right and left vagus nerve, the anterior and posterior and at least three terminal branches of the gastric nerves of Latarjet, which supply the antrum and the pylorus. When the procedure is complete, the provider controls any bleeding, removes packs and instruments, removes the ports, and closes the laparoscopy incisions with staples or one or two sutures. Terminology Esophagus: The long tubular portion of the digestive tract that stretches between the throat and the stomach. Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Pylorus: A circular band of muscular tissue at the base of the stomach; it acts like a sphincter controlling the passage of the stomach contents into the duodenum; the first part of the small intestine. Vagus nerve: Cranial nerve X, one of the twelve nerves of the brain that emerge from the lower portion of the brain (cranial nerves); it is the longest cranial nerve and is involved in sensory and motor function of the respiratory and digestive system as well as the heart. Tips A highly selective vagotomy may also be referred to as a parietal cell vagotomy. For laparoscopic truncal vagotomy, see 43651. Read Less

short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical; gastrostomy, without construction of gastric tube (eg, Stamm procedure) (separate procedure)
lay_term: The provider places a gastric tube for direct access to the stomach cavity for patients who need to be fed or have their upper gastrointestinal tract emptied directly through the stomach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, using laparoscopic technique, the provider chooses a point on the middle anterior surface of the stomach where it lies against the anterior abdominal wall. He makes a small puncture through the abdomen and then through the stomach wall, and a large catheter is inserted into the cavity of the stomach. He places one or two silk sutures to invert the stomach wall about the tube, forming an exterior lining for the tube tract. He makes sure that there is no bleeding inside the stomach. He brings the tube out through a tightly fitting stab wound in the left upper quadrant and sutures the stomach firmly to the abdominal wall. He places sufficient sutures around the exit site of the tube to prevent retraction, accidental tube displacement, and leakage. He places a tube for gravity drainage. The provider checks for bleeding, deflates the abdomen, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incisions in the abdomen with staples or sutures. Terminology Fundoplication, fundoplasty: Wrapping of the gastric fundus, that part of the stomach that rises above the point where the esophagus opens into the stomach, around the esophagus for the treatment of gastroesophageal reflux; fundoplication techniques include Nissen and Toupet. Gastric tube: A feeding tube placed into the stomach, either endoscopically, laparoscopically, or by open surgical procedure. Gastrostomy: Surgically created opening in the stomach for insertion of a feeding tube. Gravity drainage: Allowing a wound or opening to drain naturally, without the aid of mechanical suction. Laparoscopy: The provider typically makes several incisions in the abdomen, inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure, inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen, and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments; he places devices called ports to keep the incisions open, removes the ports at the conclusion of the procedure, and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. Reflux: Flow backward. Retraction: Drawing back into the wound, away from the exit site. Stamm procedure: Surgical insertion of a gastric tube with the stomach being sutured to the exit site. Tips Watch for bundles: Most commonly, providers will use this method if they already used the laparoscope for another procedure, such as to obtain a biopsy. This is important because 43653 is a designated separate procedure. This means that if the provider performs any other laparoscopic services at the same time, such as gastric bypass or bowel resection, you cannot report 43653 separately. For example, you should not report 43653 separately if the provider performed a laparoscopic fundoplication, 43280, Laparoscopy, surgical, esophagogastric fundoplasty, e.g., Nissen, Toupet procedures, at the same time, but if the provider uses the laparoscope for the sole purpose of placing the gastrostomy tube, you may report 43653 separately. short_description: Naso- or oro-gastric tube placement, requiring physician's skill and fluoroscopic guidance (includes fluoroscopy, image documentation and report) Notes: (Do not report 43752 in conjunction with critical care codes 99291-99292, neonatal critical care codes 99468, 99469, pediatric critical care codes 99471, 99472 or low birth weight intensive care service codes 99478, 99479) (For percutaneous placement of gastrostomy tube, use 49440) (For enteric tube placement, see 44500, 74340)
lay_term: A nasogastric or orogastric tube is inserted through the nose (naso–) or mouth (oro–) of the patient into the stomach via the mouth and esophagus. The physician may use radiological guidance to advance the tube to the stomach. This procedure is mainly done to aspirate stomach contents for diagnostic or therapeutic purpose, to prevent aspiration and vomiting in trauma patients, and for enteral feeding. For patients with poisoning or drug overdose, the tube is used to remove the harmful substance from the body by draining the contents of the stomach. The tube is connected to a syringe or a suction pump at the external open end to aspirate or drain the stomach contents. Explanation The physician sprays or applies Xylocaine to the patient's nostril or throat after putting the patient in an upright position that allows better alignment of the stomach and neck. A 2% Xylocaine lubricant gel may be applied to the tube to desensitize the passage. The tube is put either through one of the nostrils or through the mouth and advanced under fluoroscopic guidance. The patient is allowed to swallow small sips of chilled water to facilitate the progress of the tube. short_description: Gastrojejunostomy; without vagotomy
lay_term: The provider creates an anastomosis (connection) between the stomach and the proximal (upper) loop of the jejunum; he does not divide the vagus nerve. Explanation When the patient is prepped and under satisfactory anesthesia, the provider makes a midline incision from the xiphoid to the belly button (umbilicus) and places a self–retaining retractor to hold the incision open and expose the stomach and jejunum. He splits the transverse mesocolon (mesentery over the colon) vertically through an avascular area to enter the lesser sac. He draws the posterior wall of the stomach out through the split in the mesocolon and applies Allis tissue forceps to the fold. He also applies a pair of occlusion clamps so that bleeding or secretions do not disturb the anastomosis. He passes a hand along the undersurface of the transverse mesocolon, just below the tail of the pancreas, where the duodenojejunal flexure is found and the first loop of jejunum is situated. He picks up the first loop of jejunum and places it beside the posterior wall of the stomach so the proximal part of jejunum lies near the lesser curvature and the distal part near the greater curvature. He sutures the loop of jejunum to the stomach using nonabsorbable sutures. He then creates an opening in the stomach and jejunum and sutures the openings together.
