short_description: Excision of 1 or more lesions of small or large intestine not requiring anastomosis, exteriorization, or fistulization; single enterotomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider excises one or more lesions from the affected part of the small or large intestine using a single incision. The procedure does not require creation of an anastomosis or fistula or bringing the intestine through the skin. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the abdomen and identifies the target area of the intestine. He isolates the segment of the small intestine or colon containing the lesion or lesions. He makes a single incision in the intestines, removing all the lesions. He closes the enterotomy, called a colotomy when in the colon, using a method such as stapling or suturing. After completion of the procedure, the provider ensures control of bleeding and closes the abdominal incision appropriately. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures, anatomical or surgically created, such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end to side and side to side. Colotomy: A surgical incision into the colon, part of the large intestine. Enterotomy: A surgical incision into an intestine. Exteriorization: Exposure of an attached organ or part outside of a body cavity. Fistulization: Formation of a fistula, an abnormal passageway between structures, in a part. Tips Use 44111 for excision of 1 or more lesions of small or large intestine not requiring anastomosis, exteriorization, or fistulization; multiple enterotomies. Read Less

short_description: Enterectomy, resection of small intestine for congenital atresia, single resection and anastomosis of proximal segment of intestine; without tapering
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes an abdominal incision to remove a single narrowed segment of the small intestine from a patient born with atresia. The provider performs end to end connections between the remaining loops of the intestines. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the abdomen and explores to assess the level of atresia of the intestine. He isolates the target area of the small intestine and resects the atretic segment, retaining as much blood supply in the remaining bowel as possible. He performs an end to end anastomosis of the intestines remaining in the body. After completion of the procedure, the provider ensures control of bleeding and closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures, anatomically or surgically created such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end to end and side to side. Atresia: Absence or closure of an opening, such as a valve, or a tubular structure such as the colon. Congenital: Present at birth. Enterectomy: Surgical removal of a segment of the intestine. Resection: Surgical removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also called excision. Small intestine, small bowel: The portion of the digestive tract directly below the stomach and before the large bowel or colon; it consists of the first and second portion of the duodenum, the jejunum, and the ileum. Tapering: Gradually narrowing. short_description: Intestinal allotransplantation; from cadaver donor
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transects the affected portion of a recipient’s small bowel and then uses the cadaver donor intestine to connect the ends of the recipient’s intestines. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a midline abdominal incision from the xiphoid to the pubis. The provider dissects the surrounding structures to reach the affected area of the small intestine. He removes the affected part of the small intestine, incising through it, and clears the free ends of any debris and prepares them for connection to the transplant. The provider takes the small bowel previously harvested from the cadaver donor and grafts the donor's intestine between the separated ends of the recipient’s incised small intestine. The provider checks the circulation. The provider may apply a drain at the site to assist with healing and closes the wound with sutures in layers. The provider may perform the intestinal allotransplantation in patients suffering from Crohn’s disease, an inflammatory disease that affects the gastrointestinal tract and results in pain in the abdomen, fever, and weight loss; it mainly occurs due to bacteria that cause the body’s immune system to attack the gastrointestinal tract. Terminology Allotransplantation: Transfer of an organ or tissue between different individuals of the same species. Cadaver: Body of a deceased person. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Pubis: Forward portion of either of the hipbones that forms the front arch of the pelvis. Transects: To make a transverse cut. Xiphoid: The pointed process of cartilage at the lower end of the sternum, or breastbone. Tips Report 44136 when the provider performs allotransplantation from a living donor. If the provider performs partial open enterectomy on a living donor to obtain intestine for transplantation, see 44133. If the provider performs an open enterectomy (including cold preservation) on a cadaver donor to obtain intestine for transplantation, see 44132. Read Less

short_description: Mobilization (take-down) of splenic flexure performed in conjunction with partial colectomy (List separately in addition to primary procedure) Notes: (Use 44139 in conjunction with 44140-44147)
lay_term: In this add–on procedure, during the same session in which the provider performs a colectomy, he also mobilizes the splenic flexure, a sharp bend between the transverse and the descending colon. The provider does this to prepare a suitable length of the colon in association with partial resection. Explanation In this add–on procedure, at an encounter where the provider performs a separately reportable partial removal of the colon, he proceeds with the mobilization of the splenic flexure. The provider extends the abdominal incision. He dissects the tissues between the spleen and splenic flexure of the colon and then extends the dissection of the colon to the descending colon. The provider preserves the omentum by separating it from the colon, which allows exposure to the lienocolic ligament, the ligament connecting the high part of the splenic flexure to the bottom of the fibrous capsule surrounding the spleen. He then carefully divides the ligament to free the splenic flexure. Once all procedures for the session are complete, the provider closes the incision in the abdomen, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision in the abdomen. Terminology Colectomy: Surgical removal of part or all of the colon. Colon: The part of the large intestine that removes water from digested food, the remainder of which is turned into stool or feces; it has four parts — the ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid colon. Lienocolic ligament: An older term for splenoncolic ligament, an attachment between the lower (inferior) pole of the splenic and the splenic flexure of the colon created or formed by a thickening in the greater omentum. Omentum: Part of the membrane lining the abdominal cavity that extends from the stomach to the adjacent organs. Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Splenic capsule: Fibrous tissue covering of the spleen. Splenic flexure: Sharp bend in the colon around the spleen where the transverse becomes the descending colon. Transverse colon: The part of the large intestine that runs across the upper abdomen, between the ascending and descending segments of the colon. short_description: Colectomy, partial; with anastomosis Notes: (For laparoscopic procedure, use 44204)
lay_term: The provider surgically removes a portion of the colon and then reconnects the cut ends of the colon to restore continuity. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the target area of the colon. The provider mobilizes the colon and determines the portion for removal. The provider transects the proximal and distal sites of the target colon portion to surgically remove that part of the colon (partial colectomy). For the anastomosis part of the procedure, the provider reconnects the cut ends (such as by stapler) in an end–to–end or end–to–side manner to restore colon continuity. The provider assures hemostasis (control of bleeding) and closes the abdominal incision in layers. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two (tubular) structures, anatomical or surgically created, such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of surgical anastomoses include end–to–end, end–to–side, and side–to–side. Colectomy: Surgical removal of all or part of the colon. Colon: The part of the large intestine that removes water from digested food, the remainder of which is turned into stool or feces; it has four parts — the ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid colon. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure's point of attachment. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure's point of attachment. Transection: Cutting a blood vessel, duct, or body part to sever one part from the other. Read Less

short_description: Colectomy, partial; with skin level cecostomy or colostomy
lay_term: The provider surgically removes a portion of the colon and then brings part of the cecum (part of the large intestine) or the colon through a separate incision on the skin of the abdomen as a skin–level cecostomy or colostomy for waste removal. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the target area of the colon. The provider mobilizes the colon and determines the portion for removal. The provider transects the proximal and distal sites of the target colon portion to surgically remove that part of the colon (partial colectomy). For the skin–level cecostomy or colostomy part of the procedure, the provider creates an opening in the skin and brings the wall of the cecum (part of the large intestine) or the colon up to that opening. The provider connects the cecum or colon to the opening, such as by suture, so that the cecum or colon opens through that incision in the skin. This creates a channel for waste to leave the body, such as in conjunction with an ostomy system. The provider assures hemostasis (control of bleeding) and closes the abdominal incision used for colectomy in layers. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands that form between tissues and organs, which typically result from inflammation or injury during surgery; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Cecum: The pouchlike, first part of the large intestine or bowel; it is situated in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen just below the ileum, the last part of the small intestines; it is also connected to the appendix. Colectomy: Surgical removal of all or part of the colon. Colon: The part of the large intestine that removes water from digested food, the remainder of which is turned into stool or feces; it has four parts — the ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid colon. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure's point of attachment. Ostomy: A surgical procedure to divert urine or feces in which a provider creates a small opening (stoma) from the urinary bladder, stomach, or intestines to the body surface; examples of ostomies include cystostomy, gastrostomy, ileostomy, enterostomy, and colostomy. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure's point of attachment. short_description: Colectomy, partial; with end colostomy and closure of distal segment (Hartmann type procedure) Notes: (For laparoscopic procedure, use 44206)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes an incision to remove the affected portion of the colon and brings the upper part of the colon through a separate incision on the skin of the abdomen as a colostomy. The provider staples the lower end of the colon and leaves it in the abdomen. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the abdomen. He identifies and removes the affected part of the colon along with the blood vessels and lymph nodes. The provider brings the upper end of the colon up to the abdomen skin level and sews the colon opening to the skin through a separate incision on the abdominal wall as a colostomy. He closes the lower end of the colon with staples or sutures and leaves it in the abdomen. This procedure is also known as a Hartmann type procedure, which includes forming a colostomy and closing and leaving the other end of the bowel inside. The provider checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision in the abdomen used for the colectomy. The provider may perform the colectomy in patients suffering from colorectal cancer or Crohn’s disease, an inflammatory disease that affects the gastrointestinal tract and results in pain in the abdomen, fever, and weight loss; it mainly occurs due to bacteria that cause the body’s immune system to attack the gastrointestinal tract. Terminology Cecum: The first portion of the large bowel situated in the lower right quadrant of the abdomen. Colectomy: Surgical removal of all or part of the colon. Colostomy: Surgical procedure to create an opening in the colon, part of the large intestine; may involve connection of the cecum to a stoma, an opening through the skin. Large intestine: Long, coiled, tube like organ that removes water from digested food, also called colon, but it includes structures called the cecum, colon, and rectum. short_description: Colectomy, total, abdominal, with proctectomy; with ileoanal anastomosis, includes loop ileostomy, and rectal mucosectomy, when performed
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes the total colon along with the rectum. He connects the ileum to the anus. He may strip the mucosa of the rectum. He also may create an external opening with a loop of ileum connected to it. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the abdomen that extends from the xiphoid to the pubis. The provider dissects any adhesions present at the site. He then dissects the structures surrounding the colon and the rectum. The provider transects the intestines at the ileocecal valve, which is between the large and small intestines, and the distal part of the rectum. He may remove the mucosa of the rectum up to the level of the pelvic floor, taking care not to affect the surrounding nerves. The provider then sends the colon and the rectum to pathology for further analysis. He connects the distal end of the ileum to the anus with the help of sutures. The provider may bring a loop of the ileum up to the skin, create an opening in the ileum, and connect it to an opening in the skin to allow for emptying the intestines. This ileostomy may be temporary to allow the ileostomy to heal. He places drains at the site of the incision in the abdomen, flushes the site with sterile solution, checks for bleeding, and staples the incision used for colectomy in the abdomen. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an abdominal incision and cuts the ileum free from its attachments to the abdominal wall. He excises the scar tissue of the stoma as needed and reattaches the ileum at a new site, connecting the opening in the ileum to an opening through the skin. The provider further repairs the abdominal wall and skin at the previous stoma site. short_description: Continent ileostomy (Kock procedure) (separate procedure) Notes: (For fiberoptic evaluation, use 44385)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider creates an opening in the abdominal wall and connects it to an ileal intestinal pouch. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an abdominal incision. She then creates an ileal pouch by folding the terminal ileum, part of the intestines. Providers use continent stomas for patients who are able to manage their own ostomies and empty the intestines manually several times a day. The pouch is also called a Kock pouch after the physician who first described and performed the procedure. The provider connects the end of the pouch, which is like a valve, to the skin and secures it in place. She ensures hemostasis, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision in layers. short_description: Small intestinal endoscopy, enteroscopy beyond second portion of duodenum, not including ileum; diagnostic, including collection of specimen(s) by brushing or washing, when performed (separate procedure)
lay_term: The provider examines a portion of the small intestine for abnormalities using an endoscope, a tubular instrument with a light source and camera, which he inserts through the mouth. He includes the first and second parts of the duodenum and into the jejunum, but he excludes the ileum, the terminal portion of the small intestine, to look for a cause for gastrointestinal symptom such as bleeding and diarrhea. He takes samples of any suspicious tissue by brushing or washing the area to collect cells for laboratory analysis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places a plastic mouthpiece, also called a bite block, to keep the mouth open. He inserts a thin, flexible endoscope fitted with surgical instruments through the mouthpiece. He advances the scope toward the stomach as the patient swallows the scope. The provider guides the scope through the stomach into the first portion of small intestine, the duodenum. A small camera affixed on the endoscope sends images to a TV monitor, which provides a magnified picture of the intestinal lining and interior structures. The provider then inspects the mucosal lining of the esophagus, stomach, upper portion of the duodenum, and also the second portion of the duodenum. He inspects the area beyond the second part of the duodenum and may include all of the jejunum but not the ileum. He performs brushing or washing with a cleansing agent such as a salt solution to get samples for laboratory examination. He then removes all instruments and withdraws the endoscope. Terminology Diagnostic: Refers to procedures performed for the purpose of determining the type of disease and its causes as opposed to therapeutic, which means for treatment purposes. Duodenum: First part of the small intestine; the duodenum itself consists of four parts: the first part or upper or superior portion and the second or descending portion, the third or inferior or horizontal portion, and the fourth or ascending portion; the four parts form somewhat of a U shape with the ascending portion being a bit shorter than the descending portion. Gastrointestinal tract, or GI tract: The stomach and small and large intestine. Ileum: Third or last part of the small intestine; do not confuse with ilium, the upper part of the pelvic bone. Jejunum: The second part of the small intestine. Mucosal lining: Moisture laden membrane that lines the internal cavity of various body organs and also certain externally visible body parts like the nose and mouth. Small intestine, small bowel: The portion of the digestive tract directly below the stomach and before the large bowel or colon; it consists of the first and second portion of the duodenum, the jejunum, and the ileum. Tips Small intestine endoscopy codes 44360 through 44373 go beyond the second portion of the duodenum but not into the ileum, and codes 44376 through 44379 include the ileum; study the documentation to determine which code to report based on the additional services performed. short_description: Colonoscopy through stoma; with directed submucosal injection(s), any substance Notes: (Do not report 44404 in conjunction with 44391, 44403 for the same lesion) (Do not report 44404 in conjunction with 44388)
lay_term: The provider inserts an endoscope to perform colonoscopy through an artificial opening in the skin called a colostomy stoma. The provider performs one or more injections into the submucosa (the tissue below the mucous membrane). Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts an endoscope into the colostomy stoma. The patient has had a prior procedure to resect the colon and redirect the end to an artificial opening (the colostomy stoma) through the abdomen for waste removal. The provider maneuvers the lighted endoscope and inspects from the stoma to the cecum (first part of the large intestine) or to the connection (anastomosis) of the colon to the small intestine. The provider also may examine the terminal ileum (end of the small intestine that connects to the cecum) or the part of the small intestine by an anastomosis. The provider then performs one or more submucosal injections of any substance, typically using a needle–tipped catheter inserted through the scope. Examples of substances include botulinum toxin, steroids, India ink to mark a lesion for surgical removal, and saline to lift a lesion for easier removal. The provider removes all instruments. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two (tubular) structures, anatomical or surgically created, such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of surgical anastomoses include end–to–end, end–to–side, and side–to–side. Botulinum toxin: A bacterial toxin (poison) that a provider uses in small amounts to treat certain muscular and nerve conditions by paralyzing the muscle or preventing nerves from sending or receiving stimuli; in plastic surgery, it is used to remove wrinkles by temporarily paralyzing facial muscles. Cecum: The pouchlike, first part of the large intestine or bowel; it is situated in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen just below the ileum, the last part of the small intestines; it is also connected to the appendix. Colon: The part of the large intestine that removes water from digested food, the remainder of which is turned into stool or feces; it has four parts — the ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid colon. Colonoscopy: Examination of the colon (part of the large intestine) using a colonoscope (a tubular instrument with a light source and camera). Colostomy: Creation of a passage, usually after removal of a portion of the lower intestine, between the remaining colon and an opening (stoma) on the outside of the abdomen to divert waste into a bag worn externally that connects to the stoma; also known as a diverting colostomy. Endoscope: A stiff (rigid) or flexible tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source to examine the interior structures of a body cavity such as colon, bladder, stomach, or eye; other instruments can be passed through the channel of the scope. Ileum: Third or last part of the small intestine; do not confuse with ilium, the upper part of the pelvic bone. Mucous membrane: A membrane that lines many body cavities and tubular organs and secretes a slimy substance known as mucus. Resect: To excise (cut out) tissues, organs, or other structures, in whole or in part. Small intestine: The part of the intestine that runs between the stomach and the large intestine; the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum collectively. Steroids: A large class of chemical substances that includes hormones (a type of chemical messenger), various compounds found in the body, and drugs, including corticosteroids, a potent anti–inflammatory. Submucosal: Layer of tissue under the mucous membrane. Tips Check payer and coding guidelines. short_description: Closure of enterostomy, large or small intestine; with resection and colorectal anastomosis (eg, closure of Hartmann type procedure) Notes: (For laparoscopic procedure, use 44227)

If the patient previously underwent a Hartmann procedure, he dissects adhesions and frees up the colon, typically the descending colon, to provide as much length as possible. short_description: Proctectomy, combined abdominoperineal pull-through procedure (eg, colo-anal anastomosis), with creation of colonic reservoir (eg, J-pouch), with diverting enterostomy when performed Notes: (For laparoscopic procedure, use 45397)
lay_term: The provider removes the rectum and joins the colon to the anus using both an abdominal and perineal approach. In addition, he creates a colonic reservoir, a pouch to collect fecal waste, and a temporary diverting enterostomy if needed to allow the colon and anastomosis time to heal. Providers typically perform the procedure to treat Crohn colitis, rectal cancer, or familial polyposis. The procedure leaves the patient with an uninterrupted digestive tract so that the patient can pass stool normally. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an abdominal incision and dissects out the diseased colon and rectum to expose the bowel to the level of anal sphincter muscles. He incises the rectum at the level of sphincter muscles and incises the colon above the level of disease. He removes the diseased colon and rectum. He brings the free end of distal colon through the sphincter complex and attaches it to the anus to form a coloanal anastomosis. He arranges folds of the distal colon and sutures them together to create a pouch to replace the rectum. If he feels an enterostomy is necessary to allow for healing of the anastomosis, he opts to bring a loop of colon out through a separate abdominal incision to create an enterostomy. The provider closes the fascia and subcutaneous tissue of the abdomen in layers. He then checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the skin incisions. short_description: Excision of rectal procidentia, with anastomosis; perineal approach

Sigmoidoscopy is the examination of the entire rectum, sigmoid colon and may include examination of a portion of the descending colon. Colonoscopy is the examination of the entire colon, from the rectum to the cecum, and may include examination of the terminal ileum or small intestine proximal to an anastomosis. Colonoscopy through stoma is the examination of the colon, from the colostomy stoma to the cecum, and may include examination of the terminal ileum or small intestine proximal to an anastomosis. When performing a diagnostic or screening endoscopic procedure on a patient who is scheduled and prepared for a total colonoscopy, if the physician is unable to advance the colonoscope to the cecum or colon-small intestine anastomosis due to unforeseen circumstances, report 45378 (colonoscopy) or 44388 (colonoscopy through stoma) with modifier 53 and provide appropriate documentation. If a therapeutic colonoscopy (44389-44407, 45379, 45380, 45381, 45382, 45384, 45388, 45398) is performed and does not reach the cecum or colon-small intestine anastomosis, report the appropriate therapeutic colonoscopy code with modifier 52 and provide appropriate documentation. Report flexible sigmoidoscopy (45330-45347) for endoscopic examination during which the endoscope is not advanced beyond the splenic flexure. Report flexible sigmoidoscopy (45330-45347) for endoscopic examination of a patient who has undergone resection of the colon proximal to the sigmoid (eg, subtotal colectomy) and has an ileo-sigmoid or ileo-rectal anastomosis. Report pouch endoscopy codes (44385, 44386) for endoscopic examination of a patient who has undergone resection of colon with ileo-anal anastomosis (eg, J-pouch). Report colonoscopy (45378-45398) for endoscopic examination of a patient who has undergone segmental resection of the colon (eg, hemicolectomy, sigmoid colectomy, low anterior resection). For colonoscopy through stoma, see 44388-44408. Report proctosigmoidoscopy (45300-45327), flexible sigmoidoscopy (45330-45347), or anoscopy (46600, 46604, 46606, 46608, 46610, 46611, 46612, 46614, 46615), as appropriate for endoscopic examination of the defunctionalized rectum or distal colon in a patient who has undergone colectomy, in addition to colonoscopy through stoma (44388-44408) or ileoscopy through stoma (44380, 44381, 44382, 44384) if appropriate. When bleeding occurs as a result of an endoscopic procedure, control of bleeding is not reported separately during the same operative session. For computed tomographic colonography, see 74261-74263.

short_description: Proctosigmoidoscopy, rigid; with removal of single tumor, polyp, or other lesion by snare technique
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider examines the inner part of the anus, rectum, and the sigmoid colon using a proctosigmoid scope, a short rigid instrument with a camera at its one end. He then removes a tumor, polyp, or other lesion using a snare technique. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a rigid proctosigmoid scope through the anus and advances it to the anal canal, rectum, and the sigmoid colon. The provider then inspects the internal surface of the area for the presence of abnormal tissue or a lesion. He then uses a snare technique to destroy or remove the abnormal tissue. In this technique, the provider passes a wire loop over the predetermined, marked polyp or lesion, which the provider then shaves off using the snare. Once the provider finishes the procedure, he withdraws the scope. Terminology Anal canal: The terminal portion of the digestive tube from the rectum to the anus. Bipolar cautery: A surgical instrument that uses high frequency electric current to cauterize, or destroy by burning, lesions, or the abnormal tissue, or to stop bleeding. Hot biopsy forceps: An instrument that uses high frequency coagulation current for simultaneous biopsy and excision of polyps, tumors, or lesions. Polyp: Small growth on the inner lining of the colon. Rectum: End part of the large intestine that connects to the anus. Sigmoid colon: The loop of the large bowel above the rectum at the terminal end of the large intestine that continues to the rectum and anus. Tips Use 45308, Proctosigmoidoscopy, rigid; with removal of single tumor, polyp, or other lesion by hot biopsy forceps or bipolar cautery, when the provider removes a single tumor, polyp, or other lesion using hot biopsy forceps or bipolar cautery. Use 45315, Proctosigmoidoscopy, rigid; with removal of multiple tumors, polyps, or other lesions by hot biopsy forceps, bipolar cautery, or snare technique, when the provider removes multiple tumors, polyps, or other lesions by a combination of techniques such as hot biopsy forceps, bipolar cautery, or using a snare. He then ablates the tumor, polyp, or other lesion, which are difficult to treat even using techniques like hot biopsy forceps, bipolar cautery, or a snare. He then ablates the tumor, polyp, or other lesion, which are difficult to treat using other methods. Once the provider finishes the procedure, he withdraws the scope. Terminology Ablation: Removal of a body part or organ, or destruction of its function; in laser ablation a provider uses heat produced by adjustable focused light energy to destroy lesions or abnormal tissue, while in a radiofrequency ablation the provider uses heat produced by focused electromagnetic waves to destroy lesions or abnormal tissue. Rectum: End part of the large intestine that connects to the anus. Sigmoid colon: The loop of the large bowel above the rectum at the terminal end of the large intestine that continues to the rectum and anus. Snare technique: In this technique, the provider passes a wire loop over the predetermined, marked polyp or lesion, which he then shaves off. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass, can be benign or cancerous. Polyp: Small growth on the inner lining of the colon. short_description: Proctosigmoidoscopy, rigid; with decompression of volvulus
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider examines the inner part of the anus, rectum, and the sigmoid colon using a proctosigmoidoscope, a short rigid instrument with a camera at its one end. He then decompresses the volvulus, an abnormal twisting of the loop of the intestine, which causes a bowel obstruction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a proctosigmoidoscope through the anus and advances it to the anal canal, rectum, and the sigmoid colon. He then examines the colon where an abnormal bend is present in the intestine. Next, he uses the scope, or he introduces a stiff tube through a channel in the scope and passes it to the site to decompress the abnormal bend in the intestine. This relieves the blockage and opens the narrowed lumen of the intestine. Once the provider completes the procedure, he withdraws the scope. Terminology Anal canal: The terminal portion of the digestive tube from the rectum to the anus. Anus: External opening of the rectum where the gastrointestinal tract ends. Lumen: The interior, open area of a vessel or organ; a tubular like cavity. Rectum: End part of the large intestine that connects to the anus. Sigmoid colon: The loop of the large bowel above the rectum at the terminal end of the large intestine that continues to the rectum and anus. Read Less

short_description: Proctosigmoidoscopy, rigid; with transendoscopic stent placement (includes predilation)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider examines the inner part of the anus, rectum, and the sigmoid colon using a proctosigmoidoscope, a short rigid instrument with a camera at its one end. He then uses the channel in the scope to introduce a stent and then places the stent at the site of stricture, or abnormal narrowing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a proctosigmoidoscope through the anus and advances it to the anal canal, rectum, and the sigmoid colon. He then examines the colon where an abnormal narrowing or obstruction is present in the area of the rectum or sigmoid colon. Next, he introduces an endoprosthesis, or stent, through the channel in the scope and places it at the site. He then expands the stent against the wall of the rectum or sigmoid colon. He may also predilate the narrowed area using a balloon catheter before placement of the stent. This predilation opens the stricture of the colon or rectum and allows full deployment of the stent. Once the provider finishes the procedure, he withdraws the scope. Terminology Anal canal: The terminal portion of the digestive tube from the rectum to the anus. Anus: External opening of the rectum where gastrointestinal tract ends. Balloon catheter: A flexible tube with a balloon at the tip that can be inflated and deflated with a mechanism at the other end. Endoprosthesis: An intravascular device like a hollow stent that is placed into a duct to allow drainage through a blockage area or to act as a replacement for damaged ductal or vessel walls. Rectum: End part of the large intestine that connects to the anus. Sigmoid colon: The loop of the large bowel above the rectum at the terminal end of the large intestine that continues to the rectum and anus. Stent: An expandable mesh tube that a provider uses to open a stenosed or narrowed structure; also called an endoprosthesis. Read Less

lay_term: The provider inserts a flexible endoscope into the anus and navigates the scope to the rectum and lower (sigmoid) colon. The provider performs one or more injections into the submucosa (the tissue below the mucous membrane). Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a flexible endoscope into the anus (the external opening below the rectum at the end of the intestinal tract). The provider maneuvers the lighted endoscope and inspects the rectum (the end of the large intestine closest to the anus) and sigmoid colon (an S–shaped portion of the colon between the descending colon and the rectum). The provider also may examine part of the descending colon (the part of the colon that extends from the splenic flexure downward to the start of the sigmoid colon). The provider then performs one or more submucosal injections of any substance, typically using a needle–tipped catheter inserted through the scope. Examples of substances include botulinum toxin, steroids, India ink to mark a lesion for surgical removal, and saline to lift a lesion for easier removal. The provider removes all instruments. Terminology Botulinum toxin: A bacterial toxin (poison) that a provider uses in small amounts to treat certain muscular and nerve conditions by paralyzing the muscle or preventing nerves from sending or receiving stimuli; in plastic surgery, it is used to remove wrinkles by temporarily paralyzing facial muscles. Cecum: The pouchlike, first part of the large intestine or bowel; it is situated in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen just below the ileum, the last part of the small intestines; it is also connected to the appendix. Flexible endoscope: An optical instrument with a light at its tip that is smooth, flexible, and about as big as the tip of a little finger. Mucous membrane: A membrane that lines many body cavities and tubular organs and secretes a slimy substance known as mucus. Splenic flexure: Sharp bend in the colon around the spleen where the transverse becomes the descending colon. Steroids: A large class of chemical substances that includes hormones (a type of chemical messenger), various compounds found in the body, and drugs, including corticosteroids, a potent anti–inflammatory. Submucosal: Layer of tissue under the mucous membrane. Tips Check payer and coding guidelines. lay_term: The provider examines the rectum and the sigmoid colon using a sigmoidoscope, a flexible, narrow tube with a camera at its inserted end. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a sigmoidoscope through the anus and advances it into the anal canal, rectum, and sigmoid colon. He then examines the colon for a volvulus, a twisted loop of intestine that results in an abnormally dilated or widened area distal to the obstruction. If he finds either of these, he uses the scope or he introduces a stiff tube through the channel in the scope to decompress the intestine. This straightens the twisted loop and decompresses the distended intestine, or megacolon, distal to the volvulus. Once the provider finishes the procedure, he withdraws the scope. Sigmoid colon: An S shaped portion of colon between the descending colon and the rectum. Splenic flexure: The part of the large intestine that curves around the spleen. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider examines the anus, rectum, and the sigmoid colon using a sigmoidoscope, a flexible, narrow tube with a camera at its inserted end. He uses a channel in the scope to introduce a balloon catheter and inflates the balloon to dilate a stricture, or abnormal narrowing, of the colon. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a sigmoidoscope through the anus and advances it to the sigmoid colon. He examines the colon using the scope and checks for the presence of an abnormal narrowing. He then introduces a balloon catheter through the channel in the scope and dilates the balloon at the site of stricture to open the narrowed lumen of the colon. Once the provider obtains adequate dilation at the site of the stricture, he deflates the balloon. He then repeats this procedure for all strictures that he finds. Descending colon: The part of the colon that extends from the splenic flexure downwards to the start of the sigmoid colon. Lumen: The interior, open area of a vessel or organ; a tubular like cavity. lay_term: The provider examines the colon and rectum using a colonoscope, a flexible tube with a camera at its inserted end. If he sees any areas of abnormal mucosa or tissue, he takes samples using a brush passed through the scope or irrigates the area with warm saline and aspirates the washings through the scope. He sends the specimens to the laboratory for diagnostic analysis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a colonoscope through the anus and advances it beyond the transverse and the descending segments of the colon. The provider then inspects the lumen of the colon and rectum using the scope. He may collect specimens from the lumen of the colon by brushing or washing the surface. Brushing is a procedure in which the provider uses a soft brush to gently wipe the colon tissue or to scrape a lesion. Descending colon: The part of the colon that extends from the splenic flexure downwards to the start of the sigmoid colon. Lumen: The interior, open area of a vessel or organ; a tubular like cavity. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. Rectum: The end part of the large intestine that terminates in the anus. Transverse colon: The part of the large intestine that runs across the upper abdomen, between the ascending and descending segments of colon. lay_term: The provider examines the rectum and colon using a flexible colonoscope, a tubular instrument with a light source and camera. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs flexible colonoscopy along with placing a stent using an endoscope. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a flexible colonoscope to examine the colon for any obstruction and stricture. He places the colonoscope at the site of obstruction or stricture to determine the length of the stent the patient needs. The provider then may introduce a guide wire to assist with introducing the stent and possibly performing dilation of the site. Using the endoscopic approach, the provider places a stent at the site of obstruction to relieve the stricture. He may perform dilation at the site before stent placement, after stent placement, or both. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a diagnostic anorectal examination, or an exam of the anus and rectum, with the patient under anesthesia. He may also perform a procedure as necessary to treat any condition he finds. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses fingers or retractors to expand the anal canal. He inspects inside the anorectal area for any disease. He may complete a pelvic examination as well. He may insert an anoscope to visualize the anal canal and rectum and may use a sigmoidoscope to see the sigmoid colon and rectal lumen, when necessary. Next, he may perform a separately reportable minor procedure if necessary, most commonly for hemorrhoids, mass, or fissure repair. After completion of the diagnostic procedure, he may irrigate the area with antibiotics. Terminology Epidural anesthesia: A type of regional anesthetic where a provider injects a local anesthetic into the epidural space; the epidural injection goes to the nerve roots for analgesic, or pain relief purposes. Epidural space: The space that surrounds the dura, which is the outermost layer that surrounds the spinal canal; the epidural space houses the spinal nerve roots, blood and lymphatic vessels, and fatty tissues. Fissure: A crack or tear in mucosa. Hemorrhoids: Swollen blood vessels in the anus; also called piles; may result from straining during bowel movements or from the increased pressure on these blood vessels during pregnancy; hemorrhoids located inside the rectum are called internal hemorrhoids. Retractor: An instrument for drawing aside the edges of a wound or for holding back. Spinal anesthesia: A type of regional anesthetic where a provider injects a local anesthetic into the subarachnoid space. Subarachnoid space: The space between the arachnoid membrane and pia mater, the middle and innermost of the three membranes covering the brain and spinal cord. Read Less

short_description: Repair of rectocele (separate procedure) Notes: (For repair of rectocele with posterior colporrhaphy, use 57250)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs a forward protrusion of the rectum into the vagina. The provider performs this service for a female patient most commonly due to the vaginal delivery of a more than average size baby. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the rectocele into the muscular wall between the vagina and the rectum called the rectovaginal septum. He frees the protruded portion of the rectum from surrounding structures, pushes back the protruded portion, and sutures it to nearby fascia, providing support to the rectum. After he ensures the stable repair of the rectocele, he irrigates the rectovaginal septum with antibiotics, excises any additional vaginal tissue, and sutures the septum incision. Terminology Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Prostate: Small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males; secretes prostatic fluid, a component of semen. Rectocele: Protrusion of rectum into other body cavity, most commonly vagina or urinary bladder. Rectum: The end part of the large intestine that connects with the anus, or the external opening of the where the gastrointestinal tract ends. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. Tips For repair of a rectocele by suturing of the posterior wall of the vagina, which is known as posterior colporrhaphy technique, see code 57250, Posterior colporrhaphy, repair of rectocele with or without perineorrhaphy. In males a herniation such as a rectocele is extremely rare but normally occurs due to removal of the prostate gland. Read Less

short_description: Exploration, repair, and presacral drainage for rectal injury; with colostomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises the lower abdomen area to check for any injury to the rectum. He repairs an injury if found and drains any abscess or fluid in the presacral area, or in front of the sacral bone. In addition, he creates a colostomy with the sigmoid colon on the surface of the abdomen, which allows time to heal the rectal injury. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an abdominal incision. He incises down to the level of the abdominal cavity, places retractors, and exposes the rectum. He explores the rectum and nearby area for any injury. If he finds a rectal injury he repairs that appropriately with sutures, if possible. Next, he dissects the rectum from the sigmoid colon, creates an incision on the abdominal wall, and secures the end of the sigmoid colon out through the abdominal incision with sutures. In addition, he may also mobilize the rectum and drain any abscess or fluid in the area in front of the sacral bone, or sacrum. He may place a drain in the presacral area too through a separate incision between the anus and the coccyx, or tail bone. After the procedure, he irrigates the operative site, and closes the incision in layers with sutures. Terminology Abscess: Sac or pocket formed due to the accumulation of purulent material, pus, in the soft tissue. Anus: The distal opening of the large intestine. Colostomy: A surgical procedure that brings one end of the large intestine out through the abdominal wall through which waste can leave the body and collect in a bag. Retractor: An instrument for drawing aside the edges of a wound or for holding back structures adjacent to the operative field. Sacrum: Triangular shaped bone at the base of the spine, just above the tailbone, or coccyx. Sigmoid colon: A part of large intestine which is in ‘S’ shape just before rectum. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes an incision in the abdomen to close an abnormal opening between the rectum and the urinary bladder called a rectovesical fistula. short_description: Hemorrhoidectomy, internal and external, single column/group; with fistulectomy, including fissurectomy, when performed
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider excises a single internal and external hemorrhoid group. In addition, he removes, a fistula, or an abnormal connection between structures, and he removes an open sore of the lower rectum known as a fissure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider locates the external hemorrhoid near the anal canal and the internal portion of the hemorrhoid inside the anus. He accesses the hemorrhoid by retracting the anal canal. Next, he incises the mucosa around the hemorrhoid column and separates the hemorrhoid from the surrounding tissues. He then takes the hemorrhoid out through the anal canal. Next, he incises around the fistula and excises the diseased area. The provider may also remove a fissure by incising around it. At last he irrigates the operative sites with antibiotics and closes the incision with sutures or may leave the wounds open for self–healing. Fistula: Abnormal passageway between structures such as vessels, vessels and organs, or skin and organs or abdominal cavity. short_description: Anoscopy; diagnostic, with high-resolution magnification (HRA) (eg, colposcope, operating microscope) and chemical agent enhancement, including collection of specimen(s) by brushing or washing, when performed Notes: (Do not report 46601 in conjunction with 69990)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a diagnostic anoscopy, an examination of the anus using a small, tubular instrument called an anoscope. She uses high resolution magnification and chemical agent enhancement to improve visibility. The provider may collect a specimen or specimens of the affected tissues by brushing or washing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a scope approximately two inches into the anal canal. This code is specific to high resolution anoscopy, or HRA, which may involve use of a colposcope or operating microscope. She applies an acetic acid solution or other special stain into the anal canal to make the tissues, particularly abnormal tissues, more visible. The provider examines these tissues via the scope and takes samples of any suspicious lesions by using a small brush or washing the site with a solution. She sends the samples to pathology for further analysis. The goal of the procedure is to diagnose the presence of any cancer or other abnormal cells present. Terminology Anoscope: An instrument used to visualize the anus and lowest portion of the rectum. Colposcope: A magnifying instrument that the provider typically uses to analyze the vulva, vagina, or other female genital organs. Operating microscope: A small microscope that the provider uses in surgery to clearly view small structures, often used in eye and ear surgery. Tips The code set includes a long range of anoscopy codes. Limit use of 46601 to diagnostic HRA with possible specimen collection by brushing or washing. Don’t confuse 46601 with the code for the similar service without HRA, 46600, Anoscopy; diagnostic, including collection of specimens by brushing or washing, when performed, separate procedure. If the provider performs HRA with biopsy, use 46607, Anoscopy; with high resolution magnification, HRA, eg, colposcope, operating microscope, and chemical agent enhancement, with biopsy, single or multiple. short_description: Anoscopy; with removal of single tumor, polyp, or other lesion by snare technique
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an anoscopy, or an examination using a small, rigid, tubular instrument called an anoscope. He removes a single tumor, polyp, or lesion using a snare technique in which the provider passes a snare over the polyp or tumor and around its stalk. He then tightens the loop of the snare to grip the stalk, and pulls the polyp or tumor away from the wall of the anus. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts an anoscope, which he passes through the anal canal. Next, the provider removes a single lesion using a snare technique. In this technique, the provider passes a wire loop over the marked polyp or lesion. Then he pushes the sheath of the snare against the base of polyp. Next, the provider passes a low power current through the snare, which cuts the stalk and helps to coagulate, or clot, the blood vessels around the stalk to minimize bleeding. After the procedure is complete, the provider removes the scope. Terminology Anal canal: The terminal portion of the digestive tube from the rectum to the anus. Anoscopy: A procedure in which the provider passes a medical instrument called an anoscope through the anal cavity to examine the inner wall of the anus and the rectum. Anus:External opening of the rectum where the gastrointestinal tract ends. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Polyp: An abnormal growth originating from the mucous lining of an organ or other structure, like the nose. Rectum:End part of the large intestine that connects to the anus. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass of cells, can be benign or cancerous. Read Less

short_description: Anoscopy; with control of bleeding (eg, injection, bipolar cautery, unipolar cautery, laser, heater probe, stapler, plasma coagulator)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an anoscopy, or an examination using a small, rigid, tubular instrument called an anoscope. He identifies and controls bleeding using an injection, bipolar or unipolar cautery, a laser, heat probe, stapler, or plasma coagulator. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts an anoscope, which he passes through the anal canal. The provider examines the area and may use any of several methods to control bleeding that he finds. He may use such techniques as, chemical or electrocautery, a heat probe, laser, or argon plasma coagulation, or APC. In APC, the provider passes a high frequency monopolar current through an ionized argon plasma gas probe to coagulate the blood in an area or tissue. Terminology Argon plasma coagulation (APC): A medical procedure in which the provider controls bleeding from certain lesions in the gastrointestinal tract; also sometimes used to debulk tumors in the case of patients for whom surgery is not recommended. Bipolar cautery: An instrument that uses high frequency electric current to cauterize, or destroy by burning, lesions or to stop bleeding; the cauterization or burning uses an electrical current, which the provider passes through tissues from one electrode to another. Chemical cauterization: The burning of living tissue by a chemical substance. Electrocautery: Stoppage of bleeding using a needle or other instrument that is electrically heated. Heat probe: A small probe, usually placed on the body surface, to monitor body temperature or stop bleeding. Laser: A device that generates an intense beam of light, or other radiations from excited molecules; used in drilling and cutting, alignment and guidance, and in surgery; laser lights are also used by pain management providers to relieve pain in a particular area of the body. Monopolar cautery: Cauterization or burning using electrical current, which the provider passes through tissues from one electrode; also known as unipolar cautery. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an anoscopy, or an examination using a small, rigid, tubular instrument called an anoscope. He removes tumors, polyps, or lesions using a method other than hot biopsy forceps, bipolar cautery, or the snare technique. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts an anoscope, which he passes through the anal canal. Next, the provider inspects the area for any abnormalities and removes any tumors, lesions, or polyps that he finds. He ablates these abnormalities with an argon plasma coagulator or APC, heater probe, or other such devices. In APC, the provider passes a high frequency monopolar current through an ionized argon plasma gas probe to remove the area of tissue. Terminology Ablation: Removal of a body part or organ or destruction of its function; in laser ablation a provider uses heat produced by adjustable focused light energy to destroy lesions or abnormal tissue, while in radiofrequency ablation the provider uses heat produced by focused electromagnetic waves to destroy lesions or abnormal tissue. Argon plasma coagulation (APC): A medical procedure in which the provider controls bleeding from certain lesions in the gastrointestinal tract; also sometimes used to debulk tumors in the case of patients for whom surgery is not recommended. Bipolar cautery: An instrument that uses high frequency electric current to cauterize, or destroy by burning, lesions or to stop bleeding; the cauterization or burning uses an electrical current, which the provider passes through tissues from one electrode to another. Chemical cauterization: The burning of living tissue by a chemical substance. Electrocautery: Stoppage of bleeding using a needle or other instrument that is electrically heated. Forceps: Pincers or tongs used for grasping; also surgical forceps. Heat probe: A small probe, usually placed on the body surface, to monitor body temperature or stop bleeding. Hot biopsy: A technique in which the provider burns polyps and other tissues from the GI tract; using an instrument that uses high frequency coagulation current for simultaneous biopsy and excision of polyps, tumors, or lesions. Laser: A device that generates an intense beam of light, or other radiations from excited molecules; used in drilling and cutting, alignment and guidance, and in surgery; laser lights are also used by pain management providers to relieve pain in a particular area of the body. Monopolar cautery: Cauterization or burning using electrical current, which the provider passes through tissues from one electrode; also known as unipolar cautery. short_description: Repair of ileoanal pouch fistula/sinus (eg, perineal or vaginal), pouch advancement; transperineal approach
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs an ileoanal pouch fistula or sinus by pouch advancement through the perineum. The provider commonly constructs an ileoanal pouch for patients who have had their large intestine surgically removed due to diseases like ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, colon cancer, or injury. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider repairs the drainage tract, which is a fistula or sinus that erodes from the ileoanal pouch to the perineal area or into the vagina. He removes and closes the tract beginning at the external opening. He dissects the tract from its external origin, which is the skin of the perineum or the lining of the vagina, to its origin at the ileoanal pouch. The provider then closes the tissues. Terminology Crohn’s disease: A chronic inflammatory disease, primarily involving the small and large intestine, but can affect other parts of the digestive system as well. Fistula: An abnormal connection or passageway between two epithelium lined organs or vessels that normally do not connect; vessels and organs, or skin and organs or abdominal cavity. Ileoanal pouch: An internal reservoir; usually situated where the rectum would normally be; it is formed by folding loops of small intestine or the ileum back on themselves and stitching or stapling them together; the provider then removes the internal walls thus forming a reservoir; the provider then stitches the reservoir or staples into the perineum where the rectum was; the provider connects the pouch to the anus, allowing the patient to have a bowel movement into the anus rather than needing a colostomy bag. Perineum: The area between the anus and the scrotum in the male and between the anus and the vulva, the labial opening to the vagina in the female. Sinus tract: Abnormal passage from an abscess in the body to the skin, typically the result of infection but may also develop in the joints of patients with rheumatoid arthritis; the tract may cause swelling and purulence. Ulcerative colitis: An inflammatory bowel disease that causes long lasting redness, itching, and heat in a part of the digestive tract. Vagina: The passage in a woman's body that leads from the uterus to the outside of the body. Read Less

short_description: Repair of low imperforate anus; with transposition of anoperineal or anovestibular fistula Notes: (Do not report modifier 63 in conjunction with 46715, 46716)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs a low imperforate anus or malformed anus. He also closes an anoperineal or anovestibular fistula, creates a new anal opening, and repositions the rectal pouch into the anal opening. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider moves the out of place anal orifice, or opening, to the opposite side and makes an incision around the anus. He dissects the distal rectum circumferentially. He then makes a cross shaped incision in the normal location of the anus and creates an opening through the subcutaneous tissue of the anus. Next, he creates an opening in the remaining portion of the external sphincter. He connects the passageway in the rectum through the new opening and sutures it to the new location. Finally, he closes the incision at the previous anal site. Terminology Anal fistula: An anal fistula is an abnormal connection between the epithelialized surface of the anal canal and usually the perianal skin. Anoperineal fistula: A fistula relating to the anus and surrounding perineum. Anus: External opening of the rectum where the gastrointestinal tract ends. Cruciate incision: An incision shaped like a cross. Ectopic: Occurring in an abnormal position or place or displaced. Fistula: An abnormal connection or passageway between two epithelium lined organs or vessels that normally do not connect. Imperforate anus: A birth defect in which the rectum is malformed; it is a defect in which the opening to the anus is missing or blocked; in low imperforate anus, the anal opening is abnormally located on the perineum, not at the rectal sphincter and the opening is described as a fistula. Perineum: The area between the anus and the scrotum in the male and between the anus and the vulva, the labial opening to the vagina in the female. Subcutaneous tissue: The deepest layer of skin. short_description: Repair of cloacal anomaly by anorectovaginoplasty and urethroplasty, combined abdominal and sacroperineal approach
lay_term: The provider repairs a cloacal anomaly using a surgical technique to repair a female anorectal and vaginal defect or malformation. He also repairs any injury to the urethral wall. He combines both an abdominal and sacroperineal approach to perform this procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the perineum if the confluence of organs is relatively close to the surface, using a combined abdominal and sacroperineal approach. The provider separates the bladder, urethra, and vagina free of each other. If the bladder is swollen, the provider decompresses it. He next places the opening of the vagina and the urethra in their appropriate place. He forms a new rectum from muscle posterior to the rectum. The provider closes the incisions with sutures. Terminology Anorectovaginoplasty: A surgical technique to repair female anorectal and vaginal defect or malformation. Cloaca: A complex anorectal and genitourinary malformation, in which the rectum, vagina, and urinary tract meet and fuse, creating a single common channel; the single orifice varies in length from one to ten cm. Decompression: A procedure to remove pressure on a structure. Lithotomy: A specific position a provider places a patient in during a surgical procedures involving the pelvis and lower abdomen such as the surgical removal of a stone from the bladder, kidney, or urinary tract; a dorsal lithotomy position is when the patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups.. Perineum: The area between the anus and the scrotum in the male and between the anus and the vulva, the labial opening to the vagina in the female. Posterior: Closer to the back part of the body. Rectum: The end part of the large intestine that connects with the anus. Sacroperineal: Relating to both the sacrum and the perineum. Sacrum: A triangular bone in the lower back situated between the two hip bones of the pelvis. Urethra: Duct that conveys urine out of the body from the bladder. Urethroplasty: A surgical technique to repair any defect or injury in the urethral wall. Vagina: The passage in a woman's body that leads from the uterus to the outside of the body. short_description: Sphincteroplasty, anal, for incontinence or prolapse; child
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider reconstructs the anal sphincter of a child. The provider performs this procedure to repair a defect or tear in this muscular covering of the anal canal in a child with incontinence or prolapse. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision at the midline of the perineal area. He identifies the anal muscles that control fecal movement. Next, he excises the two ends of the muscle and overlaps the ends onto one another. He isolates the external and internal sphincter muscles, one inside the other, and sutures them together. This helps to build a separate perineal body. The procedure involves end to end sphincter suture to restore the circle of muscle. The provider commonly performs this procedure to treat fecal incontinence or prolapse. This code is applicable when the provider performs the procedure on a child. Terminology Anal canal: The terminal portion of the digestive tube from the rectum to the anus. Anal sphincter: Muscles controlling the closing of the anus. Anus: External opening of the rectum where the gastrointestinal tract ends. Fecal incontinence: Lack of control over the muscles involved in defecation, leading to involuntary loss of bowel contents; also known as anal or rectal incontinence. Midline: In the middle. Perineum: The area between the anus and the scrotum in the male and between the anus and the vulva, the labial opening to the vagina in the female. Prolapse: Dropping, falling, sinking, or sliding of an organ from its normal position or location in the body. Reconstruction: Revising a structure to approximate its normal anatomy or restoring it to its appropriate function. Sphincteroplasty: A surgical procedure to reconstruct the anal sphincter. short_description: Graft (Thiersch operation) for rectal incontinence and/or prolapse
lay_term: The provider performs a Thiersch operation, in which he places a skin graft, suture, or steel wire around the anal canal to treat rectal incontinence or prolapse. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision behind the anus and on the opposite side in the front midline. He inserts sutures, a skin graft, or steel wire with an aneurysm needle through the posterior incision and brings it forward and through the anterior incision encircling the anal canal. He then ties the suture, graft, or steel wire subcutaneously in the body fat of the ischiorectal fossa, providing a barrier for the passage of rectal contents. It narrows the anal opening and prevents the protrusion of the rectum. The provider then closes the incisions at the end of the procedure. Ischiorectal fossa: The fat filled space located on the side of the anal canal. Prolapse: Dropping, falling, sinking, or sliding of an organ from its normal position or location in the body. short_description: Sphincteroplasty, anal, for incontinence, adult; levator muscle imbrication (Park posterior anal repair)
lay_term: The provider reconstructs the anal sphincter of an adult patient. In this procedure, he covers the damaged anal sphincter muscles with the levator muscle. The provider performs this procedure in the event of an injury or damage to the anal canal, for fecal incontinence, or failure of a prior treatment. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a curved or circumferential perianal incision in front of the anus. He mobilizes, or frees the external sphincter muscle and divides it at the scar from the internal sphincter. He overlaps the torn ends of the sphincter muscles using a series of sutures. He then exposes, pulls together, and sutures the puborectalis, or levator muscle, to the anal canal. Next, he pulls together and sutures the external sphincter muscle around the anal canal to increase healing between the both edges. Finally, the provider closes the incision. This procedure is also called a park position anal repair. Terminology Anal canal: The terminal portion of the digestive tube from the rectum to the anus. Anal sphincter: Muscles controlling the closing of the anus. Anus: External opening of the rectum where the gastrointestinal tract ends. Fecal incontinence: Lack of control over the muscles involved in defecation, leading to involuntary loss of bowel contents; also known as anal or rectal incontinence. Levator muscle: A muscle which when contracts, causes the raising of a part of the body. Mobilize: Move or manipulate. Perianal: Around the anus. Rectum: The terminal portion of the anus. Scar: A mark left on the skin after the healing of an injury or wound. Sphincteroplasty: A surgical procedure to reconstruct the anal sphincter. Read Less

short_description: Hemorrhoidopexy (eg, for prolapsing internal hemorrhoids) by stapling
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes an abnormally enlarged hemorrhoidal tissue, then repositions the remaining hemorrhoidal tissue back to its normal position and staples the tissue in place. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a circular anal dilator and fixes it in the anal canal. He uses an anoscope to insert a purse string suture, which he places through the mucosa and submucosa above the dentate line. Next, he inserts a stapling device and positions it on the purse string line. After proper positioning, the provider fires the stapler to staple the prolapse and excision of the circumferential rectal mucosal ring. After completing this, the provider removes the instrument. The provider checks the stapled lines for bleeding, and if he finds any, he closes the areas with sutures. Terminology Anal canal: The terminal portion of the digestive tube from the rectum to the anus. Anoscope: A medical instrument which the provider passes through the anal cavity for examination purposes. Dentate line: A line which divides the upper two thirds and lower one third of the anal canal. Hemorrhoids:Swollen blood vessels in the anus; also called piles; may result from straining during bowel movements or from the increased pressure on these blood vessels during pregnancy; hemorrhoids located inside the rectum are called internal hemorrhoids. Mucosa: A membrane that lines many body cavities and organs; it’s also called mucus membrane; it secretes mucus. Prolapse: Dropping, falling, sinking or sliding of an organ from its normal position or location in the body. Purse string sutures: The provider makes a circular suture that is continuous, and he pulls it together to close a defect. Submucosa: The layer of tissue lying beneath a mucosa. Read Less

short_description: Curettage or cautery of anal fissure, including dilation of anal sphincter (separate procedure); subsequent
lay_term: The provider either scrapes off or burns an anal fissure. During this service, he also dilates the anal sphincter. By performing this separate dilation procedure, the provider reduces anal canal pressure. This code represents a subsequent procedure after an initial attempt. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a subsequent attempt to curettage or cauterizes an anal fissure. The provider uses a curette to scrape or scoop the fissure, or he uses a cautery technique such as chemical cautery in which he uses substances such as silver nitrate or phenol to destroy the fissure. Either technique promotes new tissue growth and healing. In a separate procedure, the provider also performs an anal dilation by stretching the anal sphincter via one of multiple methods to reduce anal canal pressure. Terminology Anal canal: The terminal portion of the digestive tube from the rectum to the anus. Anal fissure: A break or tear in the skin of the anal canal. Cauterization: The process of destroying tissue using a metal probe or cautery device usually heated by electric current; the procedure can destroy tissue, stop bleeding from small vessels, or incise soft tissue. Curette: A small spoon shaped surgical instrument used to remove material by a scraping action Curettage: The use of a curette to remove tissue by scraping or scooping. Hemorrhoids: Swollen blood vessels in the anus; also called piles; may result from straining during bowel movements or from the increased pressure on these blood vessels during pregnancy; hemorrhoids located inside the rectum are called internal hemorrhoids. Phenol: A white crystalline solid produced from coal tar and in dilute form it is used as a disinfectant. Silver nitrate: A chemical substance used as an antiseptic. short_description: Laparotomy, with aspiration and/or injection of hepatic parasitic (eg, amoebic or echinococcal) cyst(s) or abscess(es)
lay_term: The provider performs a laparotomy, a surgical procedure involving an incision through the abdominal wall to gain access into the abdominal cavity. The provider aspirates or injects liver parasite cysts or abscesses. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an abdominal incision (laparotomy). The provider then mobilizes the liver, identifies one or more parasitic cysts or abscesses, and prepares the liver for their removal. The provider also moves and protects the surrounding structures as appropriate in preparation for the removal procedure. After localizing the parasitic cysts or abscesses, the provider may aspirate them with a needle and syringe. The provider also may open the top of the cyst to aspirate the contents or inject a solution. The provider completes the procedure and closes the surgical site. Hypertonic solution: A solution with a higher concentration of salt than normal body cells to draw water out of the cells. short_description: Hepatectomy, resection of liver; partial lobectomy
lay_term: The provider performs a hepatectomy, or the surgical resection of a portion of the liver. She also partially resects a lobe of the liver. The provider performs this procedure for the treatment of both a benign or malignant hepatic neoplasm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises and enters the patient's abdomen and frees the affected part of the liver from the connecting tissues. She divides and clamps the portal and hepatic vessels associated with the affected lobe. The provider operates first at the level of the veins to free and clamp the portal structures. Then the provider makes incisions without concern for accidently incising small vessels. She divides the liver parenchyma by pressure or coagulation hemostasis. The provider then removes the portal clamp and stops all bleeding. The provider then closes the abdominal incision with sutures. Terminology Benign disease: A disease which does not progress and has little or no ill effect on health. Coagulation: The process that changes liquid blood to a gel, also called clotting. Hemostasis: The stoppage of bleeding or arrest of blood circulation in an organ or part, as during a surgical operation. Hepatic portal vein: A blood vessel that carries nutrient rich blood from the digestive organs to the liver for processing. Liver parenchyma: The key functional part the liver essential to its functioning; this is as distinct from the membrane that encompasses the liver and other supporting structures. Lobes of the liver: The liver has four lobes, right, left, caudate, and quadrate; with the right and left lobes of about equal size. Malignancy: Cancerous tissue. Malignant: Cancer, capable of spreading and causing death if untreated. Neoplasm: A new and abnormal growth of tissue, commonly a characteristic of cancer. Read Less

short_description: Donor hepatectomy (including cold preservation), from cadaver donor
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Liver allotransplantation involves three distinct components of physician work: 1. Cadaver donor hepatectomy, which includes harvesting the graft and cold preservation of the graft (perfusing with cold preservation solution and cold maintenance) (use 47133). Living donor hepatectomy, which includes harvesting the graft, cold preservation of the graft (perfusing with cold preservation solution and cold maintenance), and care of the donor (see 47140-47142). 2. Backbench work: Standard preparation of the whole liver graft will include one of the following: Preparation of whole liver graft (including cholecystectomy, if necessary, and dissection and removal of surrounding soft tissues to prepare vena cava, portal vein, hepatic artery, and common bile duct for implantation) (use 47143). Preparation as described for whole liver graft, plus trisegment split into two partial grafts (use 47144). Preparation as described for whole liver graft, plus lobe split into two partial grafts (use 47145). Additional reconstruction of the liver graft may include venous and/or arterial anastomosis(es) (see 47146, 47147). 3. Recipient liver allotransplantation, which includes recipient hepatectomy (partial or whole), transplantation of the allograft (partial or whole), and care of the recipient (use 47135).
