short_description: Donor hepatectomy (including cold preservation), from living donor; left lateral segment only (segments II and III)
lay_term: The provider performs a donor hepatectomy, or the surgical resection of the liver from a living donor. The provider resects the second and third left lateral segments only. She keeps the liver in a cold preservation until the provider transplants the liver into the body of a recipient in a separate procedure. Explanation When the donor is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places the donor in a supine position on the operating table. The provider makes an incision in the upper midline of the abdomen. The provider examines the liver and palpates the left lateral segment, checking it for any evidence of disease. The provider carefully ligates and divides the left portal vein and the left portal artery. The provider then divides the second and third left lateral segments of the liver from its attachments. The provider ensures hemostasis and then closes the incision in layers. The provider keeps the organ under refrigeration in a specially packed sealable container with some preserving solution. In this way, she preserves the liver for transplantation into the recipient body. Terminology Hemostasis: Stopping of bleeding from incisions and suture line, as during a surgical operation. Hepatic portal artery: A blood vessel that distributes blood to the liver. Hepatic portal vein: Blood vessels that drain deoxygenated blood from the liver. Ligate: Close, tie off, repair, or encircle a vessel or other structure with sutures or wire. Midline: In the middle. Supine position: Patient lying on her back with her legs extended. Read Less

short_description: Donor hepatectomy (including cold preservation), from living donor; total right lobectomy (segments V, VI, VII and VIII)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider harvests the right lobe of the liver from a living donor to be used in a separately reportable transplant into the recipient. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the abdomen, such as a midline incision that extends from the xiphoid process to the pubis. The provider dissects the surrounding structures and palpates and examines the right lobe of the liver for disease. He may perform cholecystectomy, surgically removing the gallbladder. The provider may perform a cholangiogram to check the liver anatomy to help him to insert tubes and catheters into the cystic duct. He lowers the hilar plate, which is connective tissue surrounding the area, to advance to the right hepatic duct and transects it along with its essential tissues. The provider takes care not to affect the blood supply of the bile duct and prevents injury to the remaining bile duct. He moves the lower lobe of the liver away from the inferior vena cava and ligates the right hepatic vein. During the procedure, the provider may perform an ultrasound to mark the point of connection of the right and middle hepatic veins. He ties the vessels and the bile duct with sutures. The provider uses laser or other means to control bleeding from the liver. He then holds the right portal vein, right hepatic artery, and the right hepatic vein with the help of clamps, and removes the right lobe of the liver. He preserves the right lobe with cold preservation solution. The provider then stitches the bile duct, right portal vein, right hepatic artery, and right hepatic vein. He checks for hemostasis, removes the tubes and catheters, and closes the midline incision in the abdomen with sutures in layers. The provider flushes the incision with saline solution. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Cholangiogram: A type of radiograph that providers use to take images of the bile duct between the liver and gallbladder by administration of a contrast dye. Cholecystectomy: Surgical removal of the gallbladder. Hemostasis: Stopping of bleeding from incisions and suture lines. Hepatectomy: Surgical removal of the liver or a part of the liver. Hepatic duct: A long tube that extends from the liver to the small intestine that helps in the collection of fluid called bile for the breakdown of fats in food; also called bile duct. Hepatic vein: Blood vessel that carries blood from the liver to the vena cava. Ligate: Close, tie off, repair, or encircle a vessel or other structure using a material such as sutures, wire, or surgical tape. Liver: Largest internal organ of the body that helps in metabolism, production, and storage of various substances. Lobectomy: Surgical removal of a lobe of an organ; most commonly performed in the lungs or liver. Portal vein: Vein that carries blood from one part of the body, such as the spleen, stomach, or pancreas, and circulates the blood to another body part through the capillaries, such as to the liver. Pubis: Part of the hip bone that together with the other pubis forms the front of the pelvis; also called pubic bones. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Venae cavae: The major trunks of the venous circulatory system; the superior vena cava brings blood back to the heart from the upper body circulation while the inferior vena cava brings it back from the lower body circulation. Xiphoid process: A cartilage like structure that forms the lower part of the sternum, or breastbone, and hardens during adulthood. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs backbench standard preparation of a liver from a cadaver donor before transplantation. The procedure includes removing the gallbladder, if needed, and removal of surrounding soft tissues. She also prepares the vena cava, portal vein, hepatic artery, and common bile duct for the liver transplant. The provider does not split the liver into multiple grafts. Explanation The provider acquires the donor organ previously harvested from a cadaver donor and then prepares the liver for transplant. She flushes the liver with saline or other preserving solution and then, if required, may use a scalpel to remove the gallbladder. She removes other unnecessary soft tissue structures removed from the cadaver donor along with the liver. The provider prepares the hepatic artery, portal vein, and vena cava so they’re ready for connection at the site of transplant. She then checks the blood flow through the vessels and prepares the bile duct for implantation. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Percutaneous biliary procedures (eg, transhepatic, transcholecystic) are described by 47490 and 47531-47544, and are performed with imaging guidance. They are differentiated from endoscopic procedures that utilize an access to the biliary tree from a hollow viscus for diagnosis and therapy. Diagnostic cholangiography is typically performed with percutaneous biliary procedures, and is included in 47490, 47533, 47534, 47535, 47536, 47537, 47538, 47539, 47540, and 47541. Codes 47531 and 47532 describe percutaneous diagnostic cholangiography that includes injection(s) of contrast material, all associated radiological supervision and interpretation, and procedural imaging guidance (eg, ultrasound and/or fluoroscopy). Code 47532 also includes accessing the biliary system with a needle or catheter. Codes 47531 and 47532 may not be reported with codes 47533, 47534, 47535, 47536, 47537, 47538, 47539, 47540, and 47541. An external biliary drainage catheter is a catheter placed into a bile duct that does not terminate in bowel, and that drains bile externally only. An internal-external biliary drainage catheter is a single, externally accessible catheter that terminates in the small intestine, and may drain bile into the small intestine and/or externally. A "stent," as used in this code set, is a percutaneously placed device (eg, self-expanding metallic mesh stent, plastic tube) that is positioned within the biliary tree and is completely internal, with no portion extending outside the patient. lay_term: The provider places a catheter through the skin (percutaneous placement) into the bile ducts to allow external drainage of bile, a substance produced in the liver and stored in the gallbladder that helps break down food. He performs this procedure using image guidance such as ultrasound and/or fluoroscopy, imaging technologies that display live images on a video monitor. He may also perform diagnostic cholangiography, a radiological procedure to image the inside of the bile ducts by injecting a contrast dye into the bile ducts. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, using ultrasound or fluoroscopic guidance, the provider inserts a needle into the liver via a puncture and advances it to the bile duct. Through the needle, the provider inserts a guide wire and advances a drainage catheter over the guide wire into the bile ducts above the obstruction. The provider removes the guide wire and leaves the catheter in place with the internal end secured in the bile duct. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses a biliary endoscope, or choledochoscope, a tubular instrument with a light source and camera, to visualize the biliary ducts for any abnormality or defect and obtain a sample of tissue for diagnostic purposes. She inserts the choledochoscope through an existing tube in the abdominal wall, placed in association with another procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts the choledochoscope into a T tube or percutaneous transhepatic drainage tube in the abdominal wall. She examines the biliary ducts. She may use fluoroscopic guidance and or inject dye to perform cholangiography, an imaging study, to view the ducts. She introduces forceps through the working channel of the scope and takes one or more samples of any suspicious tissues and sends the specimen to a laboratory for analysis. She then withdraws all instruments and removes the choledochoscope. lay_term: The provider removes the gallbladder through a laparoscope, a tubular instrument with a light source and camera inserted through the abdominal wall, to treat gallbladder disease. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision just below the gallbladder. She makes additional small incisions, as necessary, to allow access for instrumentation. She expands the abdominal cavity with carbon dioxide gas. She inserts a laparoscope in one of the incisions and visualizes the gallbladder. She dissects the structures surrounding the gallbladder. She clips the cystic artery and duct. She then dissects the gallbladder from the liver bed and flushes the site with saline solution. She releases the carbon dioxide from the abdominal cavity, removes the instruments and tubes, assures hemostasis and sutures the incision in the abdomen. Terminology Bile: A substance produced in the liver, stored in the gallbladder, and secreted into the duodenum; important in the breakdown of fats, or lipids; crystals in a bile study may indicate the presence of cholelithiasis, or gallstones. Biliary tract: The system of channels, or tubes, that carry bile from the liver to the gallbladder for storage and ultimately draining into the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine; the bile ducts, also known as the biliary tree, include the common bile duct, cystic duct, and hepatic ducts. Cholecystectomy: Surgical excision of the gallbladder. Common bile duct: A common path that joins the cystic duct, draining bile from the gallbladder, and the common hepatic duct, draining bile from the liver, to the duodenum, a part of the small intestine. Cystic artery: An artery that supplies blood to the gallbladder and to the deep inner surface of liver. Cystic duct: A passageway that joins the gallbladder to the common bile duct so as to allow bile to flow in both directions between the gallbladder and the common bile duct. Gallbladder: A small pear shaped organ that lies behind the liver, responsible for storage of bile. Hemostasis: Stopping of bleeding from incision or suture lines. Laparoscopy: A surgical procedure in which a provider makes several incisions in the abdomen, inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure, inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen, and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments; she places devices called ports to keep the incisions open, removes the ports at the conclusion of the procedure, and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. Tips Select a code from 47563 to 47579, Laparoscopic Procedures on the Biliary Tract, if the provider uses surgical laparoscopy in various ways, depending upon the condition in the bile duct. If the provider uses cholangiography, an imaging study using dye to visualize the biliary tract, report 47563, Laparoscopy, surgical, cholecystectomy with cholangiography. Read Less

short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical; cholecystoenterostomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider connects the gallbladder directly to the small intestine to permit drainage of bile when an obstruction in the common bile duct cannot be resolved. She uses a laparoscope, a tubular instrument with a light source and camera inserted through the abdominal wall, to perform the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the umbilicus and fills the abdominal cavity with carbon dioxide. She makes additional small incisions, as necessary, to allow access for instrumentation. She inserts a laparoscope through one of the incisions along with ports, or tubes, in the additional incisions. She assesses the gallbladder and the small intestine for any abnormality. She creates an anastomosis between the gallbladder and the proximal, or nearest, part of small intestine with staples and sutures, bypassing the common bile duct. She then irrigates the surgical area. She releases the carbon dioxide and then removes all instruments, including the laparoscope and ports. The provider then checks for bleeding and closes the incisions. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures, anatomical or surgically created, such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end to side and side to side. Bile: A substance produced in the liver, stored in the gallbladder, and secreted into the duodenum; important in the breakdown of fats, or lipids; crystals in a bile study may indicate the presence of cholelithiasis, or gallstones. Cholecystoenterostomy: Creation of a connection between the gallbladder and small intestine that permits drainage of bile in the presence of a blocked common duct. Common bile duct: A common path that joins the cystic duct, draining bile from the gallbladder, and the common hepatic duct, draining bile from the liver, to the duodenum, a part of the small intestine. Gallbladder: A small pear shaped organ that lies behind the liver, responsible for storage of bile. Small intestine: The portion of the digestive tract directly below the stomach and before the large bowel or colon; it consists of the first and second portion of the duodenum, the jejunum, and the ileum. Umbilicus: Navel or belly button. Tips If cholecystoenterostomy is performed as an open procedure instead of through a laparoscope, use 47720, Cholecystoenterostomy; direct. Read Less

short_description: Cholecystectomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes the gallbladder, a small pear shaped organ that lies behind the liver, responsible for storage of bile, to treat gallbladder disease. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the right upper abdomen and carries the incision down to the gallbladder. He dissects the structures surrounding the gallbladder and clips the cystic artery and duct. The provider dissects the gallbladder from the liver bed. He irrigates the site and inserts a drain for the drainage of fluid that may accumulate. The provider removes any instruments at the site, checks for bleeding, and closes the incision with sutures in layers. Gallbladder: A small pear shaped organ that lies behind the liver, responsible for storage of bile. Laparoscopic approach: Referring to a surgical procedure in which the provider views and accesses the abdominal and or pelvic contents with a laparoscope, a tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera to examine the interior structures of a body cavity. Because open conversion cases often take much longer than a similar procedure that is open from the start, you might be able to use modifier 22, Increased procedural services. short_description: Cholecystectomy with exploration of common duct; with choledochoenterostomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes the gallbladder, a small pear shaped organ that lies behind the liver, responsible for storage of bile, to treat gallbladder disease. He explores the common bile duct and finding a blockage that he cannot clear, he makes a new connection between the common bile duct and the small intestine to ensure free passage of bile. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the right upper abdomen and carries the incision down to the gallbladder. He dissects the structures surrounding the gallbladder and clips the cystic artery and duct. He explores the common bile duct. Unable to clear an obstruction in the distal common bile duct, he severs its distal end and reattaches it to the small bowel. He then dissects the gallbladder from the liver bed. He irrigates the site and inserts a drain for the drainage of fluid that may accumulate. He may insert a T tube into the common bile duct to facilitate postoperative drainage of fluid. The provider removes any instruments at the site, checks for bleeding, and closes the incision with sutures in layers. Terminology Bile: A substance produced in the liver, stored in the gallbladder, and secreted into the duodenum; important in the breakdown of fats, or lipids; crystals in a bile study may indicate the presence of cholelithiasis, or gallstones. Cholecystectomy: Surgical excision of the gallbladder. Choledochoenterostomy: Creation of a new connection between the common bile duct and the small intestine to restore drainage of bile in the presence of a blockage in the distal common bile duct. Choledochoscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and a working channel to accommodate additional instruments that allows the provider to visualize the biliary ducts and extract stones. Common bile duct: A common path that joins the cystic duct, draining bile from the gallbladder, and the common hepatic duct, draining bile from the liver, to the duodenum, a part of the small intestine. Cystic artery: An artery that supplies blood to the gallbladder and to the deep inner surface of liver. Cystic duct: A passageway that joins the gallbladder to the common bile duct so as to allow bile to flow in both directions between the gallbladder and the common bile duct. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure’s point of attachment. Gallbladder: A small pear shaped organ that lies behind the liver, responsible for storage of bile. Liver bed: The surface of the liver against which the gallbladder rests. T tube: A T–shaped drainage tube; for biliary tract drainage, the top part of the T fits into the duct, extending in either direction, with the base of the T exiting the common bile duct and out through the abdominal wall for connection to a drainage bag. Tips Report separately 47550, Biliary endoscopy, intraoperative or choledochoscopy, if the provider uses a biliary endoscope, or choledochoscope, to examine the bile ducts. Read Less

short_description: Cholecystectomy with exploration of common duct; with transduodenal sphincterotomy or sphincteroplasty, with or without cholangiography
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes the gallbladder and explores the common duct that carries bile to the small intestine. He repairs the sphincter of Oddi, the muscular valve that controls the flow of bile to the small intestine. He may inject dye and use X–rays to visualize the biliary ducts. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the right upper abdomen just over the gallbladder. He dissects the structures surrounding the gallbladder and clips the cystic artery and duct. The provider dissects the gallbladder from the liver bed and explores the gallbladder for the presence of any stones. He makes an incision into the duodenum and examines the sphincter of Oddi. He broadens the sphincter and repairs it using sutures in layers. He may place a T tube for the drainage of fluid, removes the instruments, checks for bleeding, and closes the incision in the abdomen with sutures in layers. Terminology Cholangiography: A radiological technique that uses contrast dye to visualize the bile ducts. Cholecystectomy: Surgical excision of the gallbladder. Cystic artery: An artery that supplies blood to the gallbladder and to the deep inner surface of liver. Cystic duct: A passageway that joins the gallbladder to the common bile duct so as to allow bile to flow in both directions between the gallbladder and the common bile duct. Duodenum: First part of the small intestine; the duodenum itself consists of four parts: the first part or upper or superior portion and the second or descending portion, the third or inferior or horizontal portion, and the fourth or ascending portion; the four parts form somewhat of a U shape with the ascending portion being a bit shorter than the descending portion. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Gallbladder: A small pear–shaped organ that lies behind the liver, responsible for storage of bile. Sphincter of Oddi: A muscular valve responsible for closing the opening of the duodenum at the common bile duct. Sphincteroplasty: Surgical repair of a sphincter, or muscular valve. Transduodenal sphincterotomy: Division of the sphincter of Oddi, muscular valve responsible for closing the opening of the duodenum at the common bile duct, accessing the sphincter through the duodenum, part of the small intestine. T tube: A T–shaped drainage tube; for biliary tract drainage, the top part of the T fits into the duct, extending in either direction, with the base of the T exiting the common bile duct and out through the abdominal wall for connection to a drainage bag. Tips Use add–on code 47550 if the provider performs uses a biliary endoscope, or choledochoscope, to examine the bile ducts in the same session as cholecystectomy to explore the bile ducts. Read Less

short_description: Cholecystoenterostomy; with gastroenterostomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider creates an anastomosis, or connection, between the gallbladder and the small intestine to provide a pathway for drainage of bile and at the same time makes a new connection between the stomach and the small intestine. He performs the procedure to restore gastric and biliary function in the presence of a condition like inoperable pancreatic cancer. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the abdomen. He assesses the gallbladder and the intestine for any defect or abnormality. He then incises both structures and brings a loop of small intestine up to the gallbladder and stitches them together, creating a passage for the flow of bile. He then creates an opening between the lower portion of the stomach and the small intestine to allow the passage of digestive contents. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision in layers. Cholecystoenterostomy: Creation of a connection between the gallbladder and small intestine that permits drainage of bile in the presence of a blockage. Gallbladder: A small pear shaped organ that lies behind the liver, responsible for storage of bile. Gastroenterostomy: Creation of a surgical opening between the stomach and small intestine. Jejunum: Second part of the small intestine. Pancreas: An organ situated between the spleen and duodenum; it produces insulin and enzymes that aid in the digestion of protein. short_description: Internal anastomosis of pancreatic cyst to gastrointestinal tract; Roux-en-Y
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider creates a surgical opening between a cyst in the pancreas and the gastrointestinal tract, usually the small intestine, in a Y shaped configuration, to provide a method for internal drainage of the contents of the cyst. He then divides the small intestine. He connects the distal, or lower, portion of the small intestine to the cyst in the pancreas via an incision in the cyst wall. He then reconnects the proximal, or upper, portion of the small intestine to the distal portion in an end to side fashion at a location distal to the pancreatic cyst anastomosis, creating the Y formation. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Roux en Y anastomosis: A type of anastomosis, or surgical connection, in which the end of one structure is attached to the side of another in a configuration that forms a Y shape; common in gastric bypass procedures but also in biliary, liver, and pancreatic procedures. Small intestine: The portion of the digestive tract directly below the stomach and before the large bowel or colon; it consists of the first and second portion of the duodenum, the jejunum, and the ileum. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider reopens a previous abdominal incision to check for complications, such as internal bleeding or infection. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision through the previous abdominal incision. He examines the organs and the structures for evidence of infection or bleeding. He ties off any bleeding vessels and takes cultures from potential sites of infection. He may drain fluid from the abdomen or perform lavage, washing out the abdominal cavity with water or saline solution, a sterile salt solution. The provider then irrigates the wound, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Culture: To cultivate the growth of bacteria or other organisms or tissue cells in an artificial medium prepared with specific nutrients and incubated under specific conditions to encourage reproduction and growth of specific types of cells. Laparotomy: Surgical incision into the abdomen. Tips Reopening of the abdomen may be either planned or unplanned. In some circumstances, the provider may know in advance that a patient will be returned for serial treatments, particularly in the case of infections like peritonitis, an infection of the peritoneum, the membrane lining in the abdominal cavity. When this is the case, modifier 58, Staged or related procedure or service by a provider during the postoperative period, should be applied. In other cases, the return to the operating room is unexpected and occurs because the patient appears to be bleeding or has fever or other indications of infection. In this case, modifier 78, Unplanned return to the operating or procedure room by the same provider following initial procedure for a related procedure during the postoperative period, should be applied. Be aware that modifier 58 results in full reimbursement but restarts the global period, while modifier 78 results in reduced reimbursement but the global period does not restart. short_description: Preperitoneal pelvic packing for hemorrhage associated with pelvic trauma, including local exploration
lay_term: The provider opens the pelvic cavity and packs the preperitoneal space with absorbent content pads to control hemorrhage from high–energy pelvic trauma. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and under adequate anesthesia, the provider makes a suprapubic vertical midline skin incision extending 6 to 8 cm up from the pubic symphysis. He carries the incision through subcutaneous tissue and fascia, which he also incises in the midline. On entering the preperitoneal space, which exudes blood, he retracts the bladder to the opposite side and quickly places 3 absorbent cotton packs called laparotomy pads into the space, pushing the first pad down into the sacrum with a blunt instrument. Visualization is difficult due to the amount of blood, but he explores the local area as well as can be done. He places 3 and up to 6 more pads to achieve successful tamponade of the hemorrhage. He closes the fascia with a running absorbable suture and the skin with staples. Other procedures, such as repair of a bladder injury, may be performed before closure. Suprapubic tube(s) may be inserted through separate incision(s). Repair of pelvic fractures would likely be performed after the patient has stabilized. These procedures would be reported separately. Terminology Hemodynamic stability: Maintenance of stable blood pressure, oxygenation, and cardiac output/blood flow; hemodynamic stability or instability is an important factor in severe trauma and the patient's ability to undergo repair procedures. Hemorrhage: Bleeding; typically refers to uncontrolled, rapid and/or excessive bleeding. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Code 49185 describes sclerotherapy of a fluid collection (eg, lymphocele, cyst, or seroma) through a percutaneous access. It includes contrast injection(s), sclerosant injection(s), sclerosant dwell time, diagnostic study, imaging guidance (eg, ultrasound, fluoroscopy), and radiological supervision and interpretation, when performed. Code 49185 may be reported once per day for each lesion treated through a separate catheter. Do not report 49185 more than once if treating multiple lesions through the same catheter. Codes for access to and drainage of the collection may be separately reportable according to location (eg, 10030, 10160, 49405, 49406, 49407, 50390). Codes 49186, 49187, 49188, 49189, 49190 describe excision or destruction of intra-abdominal primary or secondary tumor(s) or cyst(s) via an open approach. Excision or destruction of intra-abdominal primary or secondary tumor(s) or cyst(s) via an open approach includes cytoreduction, debulking, or other methods of removal of the tumor(s) or cyst(s). Codes 49186, 49187, 49188, 49189, 49190 are reported based on the sum of the maximum length of each tumor or cyst excised or destroyed (eg, ultrasound desiccation). Only the tumor(s) and cyst(s) are measured, not the tissue (eg, mesentery) in which the tumor(s) and cyst(s) may be implanted. If only a portion of a tumor or cyst is excised or destroyed, then only the excised or destroyed portion is measured. The tumor(s) and cyst(s) should be measured in situ before excision or destruction and documented in the operative report. Measurement includes only the tumor(s) and cyst(s) and not the margins. Codes 49186, 49187, 49188, 49189, 49190 are reported when the resected or destroyed intra-abdominal tumor(s) and cyst(s) do not directly arise from a resected organ (eg, small bowel mass, renal mass, liver mass) or soft tissue that may be separately reportable. When the tumors arise directly from an organ or soft tissue, only the organ or soft tissue resection or destruction procedure code from which the tumors arise is reported. For example, if a partial ascending colon resection, including small tumor implants, is performed and a separate excision of multiple small tumor implants in the mesentery of the descending colon is also performed, the appropriate colectomy code (eg, 44140) would be reported for the partial ascending colon resection and the excision of the tumor implants in the mesentery of the descending colon would be separately reported with an appropriate tumor excision code (49186, 49187, 49188, 49189, 49190). The implants that were part of the ascending colon resection would not be included in the measurement for reporting the tumor excision code (49186, 49187, 49188, 49189, 49190). Open resection of recurrent ovarian, endometrial, tubal, or primary peritoneal gynecological malignancies without lymphadenectomy should be reported with 49186, 49187, 49188, 49189, 49190. All other open resection of initial or recurrent ovarian, endometrial, tubal, or primary peritoneal gynecologic malignancies should be reported with 58943, 58950, 58951, 58952, 58953, 58954, 58956, 58958, 58960. (For lysis of intestinal adhesions, use 44005)

lay_term: The provider performs percutaneous (through a small incision in the skin) chemical destruction of a fluid collection, such as a lymphocele, cyst, or a seroma, using ultrasound or fluoroscopic guidance, imaging technologies that display live images on a video monitor. He may inject contrast material to enhance visualization during the procedure. The procedure includes the diagnostic study and radiological supervision and interpretation when performed. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, using imaging guidance, the provider inserts a needle via a puncture in the skin and advances it to the cystic structure. Through the needle, the provider inserts a guide wire, advances a catheter over the guide wire into the cystic structure, and removes the wire. He may first withdraw some fluid for analysis and inject contrast material to enhance visualization. He then injects a solution, typically ethanol (a type of alcohol) directly into the fluid–filled cavity. The sclerotherapy solution causes the walls of the cavity to scar and collapse. The collapsed wall is reabsorbed into local tissue and eventually fades. The provider withdraws the catheter and closes the incision. Terminology Cyst: An abnormal closed saclike structure containing gas, fluid, or semisolid material, has its own membranous lining delineating it from the surrounding tissue. Fluoroscopy: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Lymphocele: A cystic or saclike collection of lymphatic fluid in the body; it may be a surgical complication; the lymph system maintains fluid balance by returning fluid from the spaces between tissues back to the blood stream and supports the immune system. Seroma: A fluid–filled pocket that sometimes develops in the body after surgery. Ultrasound: The use of high frequency sound waves to view internal tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Tips This code includes imaging and supervision and interpretation when performed, so the coder should not separately code for the radiology service. Refer to CPT® and payer–specific guidelines to review requirements. Some payers may consider sclerotherapy of cystic lesions unnecessary or investigational, and it may not be covered. Check with the Medicare provider or private carrier to determine their policies. Even if not covered, you should still report the procedure for statistical purposes. Report 49185 once for each day that a provider destroys a lesion using a chemical instilled through a separate catheter. If multiple lesions are treated through the same catheter, however, you can report this code only once. Depending on the location of the fluid collection, access to the lesion with drainage as opposed to chemical destruction may be reported separately using codes such as 10030, Image–guided fluid collection drainage by catheter (eg, abscess, hematoma, seroma, lymphocele, cyst), soft tissue (eg, extremity, abdominal wall, neck), percutaneous; 10160, Puncture aspiration of abscess, hematoma, bulla, or cyst; 49405 through 49407, Image–guided fluid collection drainage by catheter (eg, abscess, hematoma, seroma, lymphocele, cyst), etc.; or 50390, Aspiration and/or injection of renal cyst or pelvis by needle, percutaneous. short_description: Excision or destruction, open, intra-abdominal (ie, peritoneal, mesenteric, retroperitoneal), primary or secondary tumor(s) or cyst(s), sum of the maximum length of tumor(s) or cyst(s); 5 cm or less
lay_term: The provider uses an open approach to excise or destroy one or more tumors or cysts in the patient's abdomen. The sum of the maximum length of the tumors or cysts is 5 cm or less. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to access the intra–abdominal area through an open approach (a surgical method involving a large incision for direct visualization of internal structures). The provider then carefully identifies one or more primary or secondary tumors or cysts (fluid–filled sacs) located in areas such as the peritoneum (the membrane lining the abdominal cavity), mesentery (the tissue that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall), or the retroperitoneal space (the area behind the abdominal cavity). The provider measures the tumor(s) or cyst(s) in situ (in their original place) to determine their maximum length before proceeding with either excision (removal by cutting) or destruction (elimination of the tumor or cyst through methods like ultrasound desiccation, which uses sound waves to destroy tissue). When necessary, the provider may perform cytoreduction, also called debulking (removing as much of the tumor as they can when complete removal isn’t possible). If only a portion of a tumor or cyst is excised or destroyed, then the provider should measure and document the length of that portion. When the excision or destruction is complete, the provider removes the surgical instruments and closes the open surgical site. This code is appropriate when the sum of the maximum length of the tumors or cysts is 5 cm or less. Tips Choose from 49186 to 49190 based on the documented sum of the maximum length of the tumors or cysts. Proper measurement is based on the sum of the maximum length of each tumor or cyst the provider excises or destroys. This measurement does not include the tissue the lesion is implanted in (such as the mesentery). The measurement also does not include the margins. Read Less

short_description: Umbilectomy, omphalectomy, excision of umbilicus (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider excises the umbilicus, or navel, primarily to treat an umbilical hernia or a nonhealing infection in this area. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the area around the external umbilicus. If the procedure is performed for recurrent hernia, the provider removes any adhesions and reduces any protruding tissues prior to further dissection. He then ligates, or ties off, and divides the blood vessels, nerves, and urachal remnant, the tubular structure that drained urine through the umbilical cord prior to birth. He removes the umbilicus entirely. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands, which typically result from inflammation or injury during surgery, that form between tissues and organs; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Hernia: Bulging of an organ or tissue through a weakness or opening in membranes or other structures. Omphalectomy: Umbilectomy; surgical excision of the umbilicus, or navel. Reduce: To restore normal anatomy; typically relates to fractures, dislocations, or hernias. Umbilectomy: Surgical excision of the umbilicus, or navel; also known as omphalectomy. Umbilicus: The navel. Tips The umbilicus is usually removed as part of another procedure, for example, umbilical hernia repair, and should not be reported with that code. Typically, this code is only reported when it is the only procedure performed in the abdomen during the surgical session. If umbilectomy is performed for recurrent hernia or recurrent or resistant infection there may be significant scarring in the area. short_description: Laparoscopy, abdomen, peritoneum, and omentum, diagnostic, with or without collection of specimen(s) by brushing or washing (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider examines the inside of the abdomen through a laparoscope, a tubular instrument with a light source and camera, to look for causes of a patient's abdominal symptoms, including pain, swelling, and organ enlargement. He inspects the peritoneum, the membrane lining of the abdominal cavity, and the fatty vascularized tissues of the omentum, a large fold of membrane that hangs like an apron across the abdomen. He may brush and wash the area to obtain cells for analysis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision at the umbilicus and uses this opening to inflate the abdomen and lift the abdominal wall away from the organs to improve visualization of the site to be treated. He then makes an additional small incision and inserts a camera and instruments to perform the procedure. He uses suction to evacuate any free fluid. He examines the organs and the structures for evidence of disease or trauma. The provider performs brushing and washing of any suspicious areas for laboratory analysis. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Brushing and washing: Diagnostic technique in which a provider uses a soft brush and irrigation to remove cellular material for laboratory analysis. Laparoscopy: A surgical procedure in which a provider makes several incisions in the abdomen, inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure, inserts a scope through one of the incisions to examine the abdomen, and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments; he places devices called ports to keep the incisions open, removes the ports at the conclusion of the procedure, and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. Omentum: Part of the membrane lining the abdominal cavity that extends from the stomach to the adjacent organs; it hangs as a fold in two layers, draping like an apron; composed of fatty vascularized tissue. Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity that attaches various organs to the abdominal wall. Umbilicus: The navel. Tips Code 49320 describes exploration of the abdomen without treatment via a laparoscopic approach. It also describes the work associated with opening and closing the abdomen for many therapeutic treatments of diseases of organs or structures of the abdomen by laparoscopy. For this reason, 49320 is only assigned when no therapeutic treatment is performed at the same operative session. This may happen when exploration finds no evidence of disease or when the disease is so extensive that no surgical treatment is possible. This code may not be assigned in addition to any therapeutic surgical treatment in the abdomen even if exploration is extensive. Read Less

lay_term: The provider examines the inside of the abdomen through a laparoscope, a tubular instrument with a light source and a camera. He places a catheter, a flexible tube, into the membrane lined portion of the abdomen to provide long term drainage of ascites, an accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity, a common complication in liver disease and abdominal cancers. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision at the umbilicus and uses this opening to inflate the abdomen and lift the abdominal wall away from the organs to improve visualization of the site of interest. He makes an additional small incision and inserts a camera and instruments to perform the procedure. He applies suction to remove any free fluid. He examines the organs and structures. He then places a catheter into the appropriate area of the peritoneal cavity. He uses a tunneler device to create a tunnel through the subcutaneous tissues and connects the tubing to the catheter emerging at another site on the abdomen. He removes all instruments, checks for bleeding, and closes the small incisions in layers. He attaches a drainage bag or other appropriate appliance to the catheter tubing at the emergence site. lay_term: The provider opens the abdomen and prepares a flap of omentum, a fatty membrane in the abdominal cavity, to fill a defect in the chest during reconstructive chest surgery, such as for a nonhealing wound. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized for reconstructive chest surgery that requires an omental graft, the provider makes a laparotomy incision to open up the abdomen. He develops the omental flap, with care to preserve the vascular attachments of the flap, or pedicle. He rotates the flap into position to fill the defect requiring repair. He sutures or staples it in place. He closes the abdominal wound in layers. The primary procedure then continues to its completion. Terminology Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Omentum: Part of the membrane lining the abdominal cavity that extends from the stomach to the adjacent organs; it hangs as a fold in two layers, draping like an apron; composed of fatty vascularized tissue. Sternum: Breastbone, at the front of the rib cage. Vascular: Pertaining to blood vessels; supplied by blood vessels. lay_term: The provider repositions a flap of omentum, a fatty membrane in the abdominal cavity, to fill a defect during an abdominal surgery. He rotates the flap into place, without disrupting its vascular supply. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized for a reconstructive surgery in the abdomen through a laparotomy incision, the provider develops the omental flap. He uses care to preserve the vascular attachments of the flap. He rotates the flap into position to fill the defect requiring repair. He staples or sutures the flap in place. He continues with the primary reconstructive procedure. Terminology Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Laparotomy: Surgical incision of the abdomen. Omental flap: A portion of the omentum used as a graft to fill defects in the abdomen and or chest cavity, usually with the omentum still attached to its vascular supply in the abdomen, through a pedicle, or stalk, and the omental graft positioned by rotating it into place; a free omental flap, without it vascular pedicle, can be grafted to other locations, like the breast or extremities. Omentum: Part of the membrane lining the abdominal cavity that extends from the stomach to the adjacent organs; it hangs as a fold in two layers, draping like an apron; composed of fatty vascularized tissue. Vascular: Pertaining to blood vessels; supplied by blood vessels. Tips Because 49905 is an add–on code, payers will not reimburse you if you report it without an appropriate primary code. Read Less

short_description: Unlisted procedure, abdomen, peritoneum and omentum
lay_term: Use 49999 to report procedures in the peritoneum and omentum in the abdomen that do not have a specific code. Explanation The provider performs a procedure on the peritoneum and omentum in the abdomen that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. Terminology Omentum: Part of the membrane lining the abdominal cavity that extends from the stomach to the adjacent organs; it hangs as a fold in two layers, draping like an apron; composed of fatty vascularized tissue. Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity that attaches various organs to the abdominal wall. Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. Include one or more similar codes, and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the operative notes or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. Your payers will consider claims with unlisted procedure codes on a case by case basis, and they will determine payment based on the documentation you provide. Read Less
